root.stem: A 27-year-old man has passed about 7 liters of urine a day and been constantly thirsty since 2 weeks ago, when he fractured the base of his skull in a motorcycle crash. He wakes several times each night to urinate. His blood glucose is normal, his serum sodium is 154 mEq/L, and his urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg. After 12 hours without water his urine osmolality rises only to 110 mOsm/kg, but 1 hour after an injection of desmopressin it rises to 520 mOsm/kg. MRI shows loss of the normal bright signal of the posterior pituitary and no mass.
root.oneliner: 27M + 7 L of urine a day and constant thirst 2 weeks after a basal skull fracture + nocturia + normal glucose + sodium 154 + urine osmolality 90, only 110 after water deprivation, 520 after desmopressin + loss of posterior pituitary bright signal, no mass
highlight: fractured the base of his skull
loss of the normal bright signal of the posterior pituitary

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Too little antidiuretic hormone (ADH, also called vasopressin), so the kidney cannot concentrate urine. The clincher: **huge volumes of dilute urine with a high serum sodium that concentrates after desmopressin**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All of these names describe the same disease. Newer guidelines rename it arginine vasopressin deficiency; the nephrogenic form becomes arginine vasopressin resistance.

nodes.q: Which hypothalamic nucleus makes most of the ADH?
nodes.note: The paraventricular nucleus makes ADH as well, but mostly oxytocin. ADH travels down the pituitary stalk inside axons and is stored in the posterior pituitary. Damage to the nucleus, the stalk or the posterior pituitary all lower ADH.

nodes.q: Which hormone is lost when a tumor destroys the posterior pituitary?
nodes.note: The posterior pituitary only stores and releases ADH and oxytocin; it does not make them. Anterior pituitary hormones (adrenocorticotropic hormone, growth hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone) are spared by a tumor confined to the posterior lobe.

nodes.q: Which injury most likely damaged the pathway in this man?
nodes.a: Tearing of the pituitary stalk by the basal skull fracture
nodes.note: Head trauma is a classic cause. After stalk injury the course can be triphasic: diabetes insipidus first, then a short phase of excess ADH release, then permanent diabetes insipidus if enough neurons died.

nodes.q: Which suprasellar tumor of children and young adults can cause the same picture by pressing on the posterior pituitary?
nodes.note: Arises from Rathke pouch remnants and often calcifies. It also compresses the optic chiasm (bitemporal hemianopia) and can atrophy the posterior pituitary.

nodes.q: Which enzyme does desmopressin switch on in the collecting duct cells?
nodes.note: Desmopressin is an ADH (V2 receptor) agonist. The V2 receptor couples to a stimulatory G protein (Gs), which activates adenylyl cyclase; cyclic AMP and protein kinase A then move aquaporin-2 water channels from vesicles into the apical membrane. Without ADH the collecting duct stays waterproof.

nodes.q: Without ADH, which kind of urine does the kidney make?
nodes.a: A large volume of dilute (hypotonic) urine
nodes.note: Water is not reabsorbed in the collecting duct, so urine osmolality falls below serum osmolality. The thick ascending limb never reabsorbs water, so it does not change this.

nodes.q: Why is his serum sodium high?
nodes.a: He loses free water faster than he can replace it
nodes.note: Pure water loss raises serum sodium and serum osmolality. Thirst is the only protection, so a patient who cannot drink (for example after a head injury) becomes severely dehydrated; severe high sodium shrinks the brain and can tear bridging veins and cause bleeding.

nodes.q: Which complication follows if the high sodium is corrected too fast with hypotonic fluid?
nodes.note: Brain cells adapt to a high sodium by taking up solutes; rapid fall of serum osmolality pulls water into them.

nodes.q: Which test best separates this disease from the nephrogenic form?
nodes.a: Water deprivation test followed by an injection of desmopressin
nodes.note: Central disease: urine osmolality rises by **more than 50% after desmopressin**. Nephrogenic disease: little or no rise. Primary polydipsia: urine concentrates during water deprivation itself.

nodes.q: Which drug replaces the missing hormone?
nodes.a: Desmopressin (DDAVP), by nose or by mouth
nodes.note: A selective V2 agonist, so it has little effect on blood pressure. Thiazide diuretics are used for the nephrogenic form, not here.

nodes.q: His dilute urine could suggest nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Urine stays dilute after desmopressin**; ADH level high; lithium, hypercalcemia or an inherited V2 receptor defect
**Urine osmolality rises by more than 50% after desmopressin**; ADH level low; head injury or a pituitary or hypothalamic lesion

nodes.note: The trap: both give polyuria, thirst, a high sodium and dilute urine; only the desmopressin response separates them.

nodes.q: Constant thirst and dilute urine could suggest primary polydipsia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Serum sodium low-normal** because he drinks too much; urine concentrates normally when water is withheld
**Serum sodium high-normal or high**; urine stays dilute during water deprivation until desmopressin is given

nodes.q: His abnormal sodium points to a disorder of ADH, which could suggest the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low serum sodium + concentrated urine** (excess ADH, water kept)
**High serum sodium + dilute urine** (too little ADH, water lost)

nodes.q: Polyuria and thirst could suggest diabetes mellitus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High blood glucose with glucose in the urine**; osmotic diuresis, urine is not very dilute
**Normal blood glucose + urine osmolality 90**

nodes.q: His high sodium could come from other diseases. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Hypertension + low potassium + high aldosterone with low renin**

root.stem: A 22-year-old woman has had 10 days of constant thirst and passes 6.5 liters of urine a day, waking several times each night to urinate. She has taken lithium carbonate for 2 years for bipolar disorder, and the dose was raised 6 months ago. Her blood glucose is normal, her serum sodium and serum osmolality are high, her urine osmolality is 75 mOsm/kg, and her blood ADH (antidiuretic hormone) level is high. After an injection of desmopressin her urine osmolality stays at 80 mOsm/kg. She has no flank pain and no hematuria.
root.oneliner: 22F + thirst, 6.5 L of urine a day, nocturia + lithium for bipolar disorder, dose raised 6 months ago + normal glucose + high sodium and serum osmolality + urine osmolality 75, 80 after desmopressin + high ADH + no flank pain or hematuria
highlight: blood ADH (antidiuretic hormone) level is high
no flank pain and no hematuria

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The collecting duct does not respond to antidiuretic hormone (ADH). The clincher: **dilute urine that stays dilute after desmopressin, with a high ADH level**.

nodes.q: Why is her blood ADH level high?
nodes.a: The high serum osmolality stimulates its release, but the kidney cannot respond
nodes.note: In central diabetes insipidus the same stimulus meets a low ADH level.

nodes.q: Which test shows that the kidney, and not the brain, is at fault?
nodes.a: Water deprivation test followed by desmopressin, with urine osmolality that barely rises
nodes.note: A rise of more than 50% means central disease; little or no rise (under about 10%) means nephrogenic disease.

nodes.q: How does lithium cause this?
nodes.a: It blocks the ADH-stimulated, cyclic AMP (cAMP)-mediated response in the collecting duct, so aquaporin-2 channels are not inserted
nodes.note: Lithium enters principal cells through the epithelial sodium channel and lowers aquaporin-2 production.

nodes.q: Which cells of the collecting duct carry the receptor for ADH?
nodes.note: The V2 receptor signals through a Gs protein, adenylyl cyclase and cyclic AMP.

nodes.q: Which high blood mineral level can also damage the collecting duct response?
nodes.note: Low potassium (hypokalemia) and the drug demeclocycline do the same, as does relief of urinary obstruction. Chronic lithium damage can last after the drug is stopped.

nodes.q: Which inherited form is the commonest?
nodes.a: X-linked recessive mutation of the V2 receptor gene
nodes.note: Seen mainly in boys, often with polyuria, fever from dehydration and failure to thrive in infancy. A rarer autosomal form affects the aquaporin-2 gene.

nodes.q: Which diuretic class, with a low-sodium diet, paradoxically cuts her urine volume?
nodes.note: Mild volume depletion makes the proximal tubule reabsorb more sodium and water, so less fluid reaches the collecting duct. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) also reduce urine volume. Caution: thiazides raise the lithium level, so in her case lithium is stopped or the level watched closely.

nodes.q: Which potassium-sparing drug is used for lithium-induced disease because it blocks lithium entry into the cells?
nodes.note: It blocks the epithelial sodium channel.

nodes.q: Her dilute urine could suggest central diabetes insipidus, with decreased secretion of ADH. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Urine osmolality rises by more than 50% after desmopressin**; ADH level low; head injury or pituitary lesion
**Urine stays dilute after desmopressin + high ADH level**; lithium

nodes.note: The trap: the history of thirst and nocturia is identical.

nodes.q: Her thirst could suggest primary polydipsia, in which washout of the renal gradient dilutes the urine. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low-normal serum sodium**; urine concentrates when water is withheld
**High serum sodium**; urine stays dilute despite water deprivation and desmopressin

nodes.q: Her polyuria could come from an osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High blood glucose, glucose in the urine**
**Normal blood glucose + urine osmolality 75**

nodes.q: Years of a kidney-toxic drug could suggest renal papillary (medullary) necrosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flank pain, hematuria and sloughed papillae** after NSAID use, sickle cell disease or diabetes
**Painless polyuria with a normal urinalysis**

root.stem: A 73-year-old man who has had type 2 diabetes mellitus for 15 years and hypertension is brought in by his wife because of 8 months of dry skin, marked cold intolerance, constipation, a 4-kg weight gain, and slow speech. He now needs a long time to get out of bed each morning and keeps misplacing his keys. His mood is cheerful, his gait is normal, and he has no urinary incontinence. His tongue is enlarged, his voice is hoarse, his pulse is 54/min, and the ankle reflexes show slow relaxation. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) is high and free thyroxine (T4) is low. He is started on full-replacement thyroxine. Two months later, once the symptoms have settled, he begins calcium carbonate for osteopenia, and his symptoms return with a rising TSH.
root.oneliner: 73M + type 2 diabetes and hypertension + 8 months of dry skin, cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain + slow speech and forgetfulness, cheerful mood, normal gait, no incontinence + big tongue, hoarse voice, pulse 54, slow ankle reflex relaxation + high TSH, low free T4 + symptoms return after starting calcium carbonate on thyroxine
highlight: dry skin, marked cold intolerance, constipation
is high and free thyroxine (T4) is low

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The thyroid gland itself makes too little hormone, so the pituitary pushes out more thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). The clincher: **high TSH with low free thyroxine (T4)** plus cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, weight gain and slowing.

nodes.q: Before any thyroid results were back, which single blood test would best establish the cause of his slowing and forgetfulness?
nodes.note: Hypothyroidism is a reversible cause of cognitive decline. A low free T4 then confirms it.

nodes.q: What is the usual cause in iodine-sufficient countries?
nodes.note: Autoimmune destruction with anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies, lymphocytes with germinal centers and Hurthle cells on biopsy.

nodes.q: Which dietary lack is the commonest cause worldwide?
nodes.note: Low iodine lowers hormone output, TSH rises and the gland enlarges (goiter).

nodes.q: Which substance builds up in the skin and tongue to give the dry, doughy skin and large tongue?
nodes.note: This is myxedema. The deposits attract water.

nodes.q: Why does he feel cold and gain weight without eating more?
nodes.a: Lower basal metabolic rate, with less Na+/K+-ATPase activity and heat production
nodes.note: Thyroid hormone raises oxygen use and heat output in nearly every tissue, and slows gut transit when low.

nodes.q: Which blood lipid rises because the liver has fewer receptors to clear it?
nodes.note: Hypothyroidism accelerates atherosclerosis; check TSH in unexplained dyslipidemia.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening end stage appears after an infection, cold or sedatives in untreated disease?
nodes.note: Hypothermia, bradycardia, hypoventilation, low sodium and altered consciousness. Treat with intravenous levothyroxine plus hydrocortisone.

nodes.q: Into which more active hormone do his tissues convert the thyroxine he is given?
nodes.note: 5'-deiodinase removes one iodine from thyroxine (T4). T3 binds a nuclear receptor and changes gene transcription. Levothyroxine is taken on an empty stomach, the dose is adjusted to the TSH, and older men with coronary risk start low and go slowly.

nodes.q: Which cardiac event is he at risk of in the first month of full-dose thyroxine?
nodes.note: Thyroid hormone raises heart rate and contractility, increasing oxygen demand in coronary arteries that are already narrowed.

nodes.q: Why did the TSH rise after the calcium carbonate was added?
nodes.a: Calcium binds levothyroxine in the gut and decreases its absorption
nodes.note: Iron, aluminum antacids, sucralfate and cholestyramine do the same; separate them from levothyroxine by about 4 hours.

nodes.q: His symptoms could return because an enzyme inducer speeds up the breakdown of levothyroxine. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **New phenytoin, carbamazepine or rifampin** raising hepatic metabolism of thyroxine
**Calcium carbonate taken with levothyroxine**; symptoms return a few weeks after the supplement is started

nodes.q: His slowing and forgetfulness could be a primary brain disease. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Gradual memory loss with normal TSH and no cold intolerance**
Normal thyroid tests would be expected
**Low mood and loss of interest; weight loss and insomnia are usual**
Pupil changes and a positive serology

nodes.q: His TSH is high. Where would the fault lie if instead the TSH were low?
nodes.note: The thyrotropin-releasing hormone test tells hypothalamic from pituitary disease. Dietary iodine deficiency and thyroid hormone resistance both raise TSH.

root.stem: A 45-year-old man has had 3 years of an enlarging nose, coarsening facial features, and a rising shoe size. He has frequent headaches, diffuse joint pain, generalized weakness, pain in both hands with trouble picking up small objects, and jaw pain that is worse on chewing. His blood pressure is 150/92 mm Hg. Serum insulin-like growth factor-1 (IGF-1), glucose and triglyceride levels are all raised. MRI shows a pituitary adenoma. He has no weight gain on his trunk, no purple stretch marks and no breast discharge.
root.oneliner: 45M + 3 years of enlarging nose, coarse face, rising shoe size + headaches, joint pain, weakness + hand pain, trouble picking up small objects + jaw pain on chewing + high IGF-1, glucose, triglycerides + pituitary adenoma + no trunk weight gain, stretch marks or breast discharge
highlight: jaw pain that is worse on chewing
glucose and triglyceride levels are all raised
no weight gain on his trunk, no purple stretch marks and no breast discharge

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Excess growth hormone (GH) in an adult whose growth plates have closed. The clincher: **enlarging hands, feet and nose with coarse features and a high IGF-1 level**.

nodes.q: Which blood test is used to screen for it?
nodes.note: Growth hormone swings through the day, but IGF-1 (made in the liver under GH) stays steady and reflects the average level.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Failure of GH to fall after an oral glucose load
nodes.note: Normal people suppress GH after glucose. Then MRI shows the tumor.

nodes.q: Which cell type of the anterior pituitary forms the adenoma?
nodes.note: Acidophilic (eosinophilic) cells, often densely granulated. Some tumors also make prolactin.

nodes.q: In many of these tumors the alpha subunit of the stimulatory G protein (Gs) has lost its GTPase activity. Which enzyme stays switched on?
nodes.note: An activating GNAS mutation (about 40% of tumors) keeps Gs bound to GTP, so adenylyl cyclase keeps making cyclic AMP, as if growth hormone-releasing hormone were always present. The normal GH receptor on target cells signals through the Janus kinase pathway.

nodes.q: Why are his glucose and triglycerides high?
nodes.a: GH works against insulin: less glucose uptake in muscle, more lipolysis in fat and more gluconeogenesis in the liver
nodes.note: Excess GH can lead to diabetes mellitus.

nodes.q: Which nerve compression explains the hand pain and trouble picking up small objects?
nodes.a: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
nodes.note: Soft tissue overgrowth at the wrist.

nodes.q: Which complication is the main cause of death?
nodes.note: Left ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure. Sleep apnea and diabetes add to the risk.

nodes.q: Which cancer screening is done more often in these patients?
nodes.a: Colonoscopy, because of colon polyps and cancer
nodes.note: Raised IGF-1 promotes growth of colonic epithelium.

nodes.q: Which visual field defect follows when the adenoma grows upward?
nodes.note: The tumor compresses the optic chiasm from below.

nodes.q: What is the first-line treatment?
nodes.note: Medical therapy is used when surgery does not cure.

nodes.q: Which drug class lowers GH by acting on somatostatin receptors?
nodes.note: Cabergoline (a dopamine agonist) has a lesser effect.

nodes.q: Which drug blocks the GH receptor and lowers IGF-1?
nodes.note: A GH analog that blocks the receptor. Monitor IGF-1; GH levels stay high on this drug.

nodes.q: His coarse features, weakness and joint pains could suggest hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cold intolerance, weight gain, slow reflex relaxation and a high thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)**; no growth of the hands and feet
**Larger hands, feet and shoe size + high IGF-1 + pituitary adenoma**

nodes.note: The trap: both give coarse features, an enlarged tongue, arthralgia and weakness.

nodes.q: His high glucose and hypertension could suggest Cushing disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Central obesity, purple striae, moon face** and high cortisol after the dexamethasone test
**Rising shoe size and ring size + high IGF-1**; no truncal obesity or striae

nodes.q: His headaches and pituitary adenoma could suggest prolactinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Galactorrhea and low libido** with a high prolactin
**Enlarged extremities with a high IGF-1**; no breast discharge

nodes.q: Large hands and feet could come from other diseases. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Excess GH before the growth plates close: very tall child or teenager**
**High alkaline phosphatase with a thick skull and hearing loss; IGF-1 normal**

root.stem: A 58-year-old man who smokes has had 6 months of a dry cough, darkening skin and swollen feet. He now has difficulty getting up from a chair. His blood pressure is 160/98 mm Hg and he has muscle wasting, pedal edema and global weakness of the proximal limb muscles. Reflexes and sensation are normal, and repeated effort does not make the weakness better. Serum potassium is 2.9 mEq/L and glucose is 150 mg/dL; sodium and calcium are normal. Adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) and cortisol are both high, and a high dose of dexamethasone does not lower the cortisol. A chest x-ray shows a large mass in the left hilum, and an endobronchial biopsy shows small blue cells.
root.oneliner: 58M smoker + 6 months of cough, dark skin, swollen feet + trouble rising from a chair + BP 160/98, proximal weakness, normal reflexes, no improvement with effort + potassium 2.9, glucose 150, normal sodium and calcium + high ACTH and cortisol not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone + hilar mass, small blue cells
highlight: difficulty getting up from a chair
repeated effort does not make the weakness better
large mass in the left hilum

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Cushing syndrome from a tumor outside the pituitary that makes adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH). The clincher: **high ACTH and cortisol not suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone, with hypokalemia and hypertension, in a patient with a lung tumor**. Because the cortisol rise is fast, weight loss, muscle wasting, edema and hypokalemia often outweigh the classic moon face and striae.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which tumor is the commonest source?
nodes.note: A neuroendocrine tumor of the central bronchi that makes many hormones.

nodes.q: Which slower-growing lung tumor of neuroendocrine cells can cause the same syndrome?
nodes.note: Carcinoid syndrome is rare unless it spreads to the liver.

nodes.q: From which precursor protein are both ACTH and the pigment-stimulating hormone cut?
nodes.note: Cleavage of POMC gives ACTH and melanocyte-stimulating hormone, and ACTH itself acts on melanocyte receptors. Pituitary Cushing disease also darkens the skin when ACTH is high; primary adrenal Cushing syndrome does not.

nodes.q: Why does he have hypertension and a low potassium?
nodes.a: Cortisol is so high that it overwhelms 11-beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 and activates the mineralocorticoid receptor
nodes.note: This salt-retaining effect is stronger in ectopic ACTH than in pituitary disease.

nodes.q: Why is it hard for him to rise from a chair?
nodes.a: Cortisol breaks down muscle protein, causing proximal steroid myopathy
nodes.note: Cortisol also raises glucose by gluconeogenesis, shown by his glucose of 150.

nodes.q: What change would the adrenal glands show?
nodes.note: ACTH drives growth of the zona fasciculata and reticularis.

nodes.q: Which test separates this from pituitary Cushing disease?
nodes.a: High-dose dexamethasone suppression test, where cortisol stays high
nodes.note: A pituitary adenoma still partly suppresses; the ectopic tumor does not.

nodes.q: Which sampling of veins would show no step-up of ACTH from the pituitary side?
nodes.note: Used when the dexamethasone test and MRI disagree.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?
nodes.note: If the tumor cannot be removed, bilateral adrenalectomy is an option.

nodes.q: Which drug blocks 11-beta-hydroxylase, the last step of cortisol synthesis, while the tumor is treated?
nodes.note: Ketoconazole and osilodrostat also block adrenal steroid synthesis; mitotane destroys adrenal cortex cells.

nodes.q: His proximal weakness and lung cancer could suggest Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Weakness that improves with repeated effort + absent reflexes + antibodies to presynaptic calcium channels**
**Weakness without improvement + normal reflexes + high ACTH, cortisol, hypokalemia and hypertension**

nodes.note: The trap: both occur with small cell lung carcinoma and cause proximal weakness.

nodes.q: The high ACTH could come from the pituitary. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cortisol falls after high-dose dexamethasone**; no lung mass; milder hypokalemia
**Cortisol does not fall + lung mass + marked hypokalemia**

nodes.q: Cortisol excess could come from the adrenal gland itself. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **ACTH low or undetectable** because high cortisol suppresses the pituitary; unilateral adrenal mass
**ACTH high + bilateral adrenal hyperplasia + hyperpigmentation**

nodes.q: Other tumor-related hormone syndromes could also present with this lung mass. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Low renin and high aldosterone, no lung mass**
Hyperpigmentation, high ACTH and a lung mass
Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion from the tumor
**High calcium in a squamous cell lung carcinoma**

highlight: severe neck pain that spreads to the jaw and ear
sore throat and cough ended 2 weeks ago
radioactive iodine uptake is very low

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A painful thyroid inflammation that follows a viral illness. The clincher: **tender thyroid after a viral infection, thyrotoxicosis with low radioactive iodine uptake and a high ESR**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Also called subacute painful thyroiditis.

nodes.q: Why is she thyrotoxic although the iodine uptake is low?
nodes.a: Inflamed follicles leak preformed hormone, and the low TSH shuts off new hormone synthesis
nodes.note: The gland is destroyed, not overworking.

nodes.q: Which cells surround fragments of colloid in the granulomas on biopsy?
nodes.note: Follicles are destroyed and colloid is lost; the inflammation is patchy.

nodes.q: Which serum protein released from the damaged follicles is high, unlike in thyrotoxicosis from taking thyroid pills?
nodes.note: Factitious thyrotoxicosis suppresses the gland, so thyroglobulin is low. Antithyroid antibodies are usually absent or low here.

nodes.q: Which drugs relieve the pain?

nodes.note: Prednisone for severe pain. Hormone is not being newly made, so antithyroid drugs like methimazole do not help.

nodes.q: Which drug class controls her palpitations and fast pulse until the thyrotoxic phase passes?
nodes.note: Propranolol also slightly reduces conversion of T4 to T3. Thionamides do not help because no new hormone is being made.

nodes.q: What happens to her thyroid function over the next months?
nodes.a: A hypothyroid phase, then recovery to normal
nodes.note: Most patients recover fully; a few stay hypothyroid.

nodes.q: Her palpitations and thyrotoxicosis could suggest Graves disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painless diffuse goiter + exophthalmos + high iodine uptake**; thyroid-stimulating antibodies
**Painful tender thyroid after a viral illness + high ESR + low iodine uptake**

root.stem: A 24-year-old woman comes in for counseling before she tries to conceive. Her periods come at irregular 25- to 42-day intervals. She is 170 cm tall and weighs 100 kg (BMI 35 kg/m2). She has dark hair on the upper lip and chin, acne on the face, chest and back, and velvety brown thickened skin at the neck and armpits. Her voice has not changed, she has no purple stretch marks, no breast discharge and no cold intolerance, and her blood pressure is normal. Morning 17-hydroxyprogesterone, prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels are normal.
root.oneliner: 24F + irregular periods every 25 to 42 days + BMI 35 + hair on upper lip and chin + acne + velvety thickened skin at neck and armpits + unchanged voice, no purple stretch marks, no breast discharge, no cold intolerance + wants to conceive + normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone, prolactin and TSH
highlight: dark hair on the upper lip and chin
acne on the face, chest and back
velvety brown thickened skin at the neck and armpits
17-hydroxyprogesterone, prolactin and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The commonest cause of anovulation in young women. The clincher: **irregular cycles + signs of androgen excess (hirsutism, acne) + insulin resistance (acanthosis nigricans) after other causes are excluded**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: How many of the three Rotterdam criteria are needed for diagnosis?
nodes.note: The three: irregular or absent ovulation, androgen excess (clinical or in blood) and polycystic-appearing ovaries on ultrasound. She already has the first two. Other causes (thyroid disease, high prolactin, late-onset congenital adrenal hyperplasia) must be excluded.

nodes.q: Which metabolic abnormality drives the disease and explains her neck skin?
nodes.a: Insulin resistance with high insulin levels (hyperinsulinemia)
nodes.note: Insulin acts on ovarian theca cells to make androgens and lowers sex hormone-binding globulin, so free testosterone rises.

nodes.q: Which gonadotropin pattern is typical?
nodes.a: High luteinizing hormone (LH) relative to follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)
nodes.note: LH drives androgen production by theca cells; low FSH stalls follicle maturation, so ovulation fails. Testosterone is raised.

nodes.note: A group of inherited, single-gene forms of diabetes, usually starting before about 25 years of age, without insulin resistance. The clincher: **mild, stable high fasting glucose in a thin, antibody-negative patient with diabetes in each generation of her family**.

nodes.q: Which inheritance pattern fits her mother and sister being affected?

**Normal weight + mild stable hyperglycemia + affected mother and sister**

nodes.note: An inherited syndrome of several endocrine tumors. The clincher: **medullary thyroid carcinoma + pheochromocytoma + hyperparathyroidism**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?

nodes.q: From which embryonic tissue do the cells of this thyroid carcinoma arise?
nodes.note: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from parafollicular C cells, which come from the neural crest (via the ultimobranchial body), not from the follicular epithelium.

nodes.q: Which hormone made by the tumor cells is measured to watch for recurrence?
nodes.note: The amyloid between the cells is derived from calcitonin. Carcinoembryonic antigen is a second marker.

nodes.q: Which gene carries the activating mutation?
nodes.note: A receptor tyrosine kinase on chromosome 10; autosomal dominant inheritance. Loss-of-function RET mutations cause Hirschsprung disease, which can occur in MEN2A families.

nodes.q: Which third gland explains her calcium of 11.4 mg/dL?

nodes.q: Which hormones does her adrenal tumor secrete?

Hemoglobin and total protein are normal, she has not lost weight, and no one in her family has had high calcium. A hand x-ray shows thinning of the outer surface of the finger bones, and a technetium-99m sestamibi scan shows a single 1.2-cm nodule behind the thyroid. nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The parathyroid glands make too much parathyroid hormone (PTH) on their own. The clincher: **high calcium with high PTH and low phosphate**, with kidney stones, bone disease, abdominal complaints and low mood.

nodes.q: Which lesion most likely produced the single nodule on her scan?
nodes.a: A single parathyroid adenoma (chief cell adenoma)
nodes.note: About 85% of cases. Hyperplasia of all four glands causes most of the rest, and carcinoma is rare. The sestamibi scan lights up the one overactive gland.

nodes.q: Which gene, mutated in many sporadic adenomas, is also the gene behind the inherited syndrome of parathyroid, pituitary and pancreatic tumors?
nodes.note: In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 several glands overgrow together. Cyclin D1 overexpression is the other common change in sporadic adenomas.

nodes.q: Why is her phosphate low?
nodes.a: PTH blocks phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule, so phosphate is lost in the urine
nodes.note: High calcium with low phosphate is the key pairing. Vitamin D excess raises phosphate instead.

nodes.q: Which active vitamin D form does PTH make more of in the kidney?
nodes.note: Calcitriol raises calcium absorption in the gut; PTH has no direct action on the gut. PTH also raises calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule.

nodes.q: Osteoclasts have no PTH receptor. How does PTH still raise their activity?
nodes.a: It acts on osteoblasts, which signal osteoclasts by RANK ligand, the ligand of the receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B (paracrine stimulation)
nodes.note: More osteoclast maturation and activity pulls calcium out of bone. Constant PTH exposure destroys bone, while short daily doses (teriparatide) build it.

nodes.q: Which bone disease results from years of excess PTH?
nodes.note: Subperiosteal resorption of the finger bones is the earliest x-ray sign; later brown tumors (osteoclast-rich cysts with old blood), a salt-and-pepper skull and generalized osteopenia. Alkaline phosphatase rises from osteoblast activity, and vertebral compression fractures cause sudden back pain.

nodes.q: Which kidney problem explains her stone?
nodes.a: Calcium stones (calcium oxalate or calcium phosphate)
nodes.note: Hypercalciuria: the filtered calcium load exceeds the extra reabsorption PTH causes. Nephrocalcinosis can follow.

nodes.q: Which rhyme summarizes the symptoms of hypercalcemia?
nodes.a: Stones, bones, groans, thrones and psychiatric overtones
nodes.note: Stones (kidney stones; gallstones are also more common), bones (pain, osteitis fibrosa cystica), groans (abdominal pain, nausea, peptic ulcer, pancreatitis), thrones (polyuria, constipation), psychiatric overtones (low mood up to coma).

nodes.q: Why does her high calcium make her thirsty and pass large volumes of urine?
nodes.a: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus: high calcium blunts the collecting duct's response to antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
nodes.note: Calcium acts on the calcium-sensing receptor of the thick ascending limb and collecting duct, so less water is reabsorbed. The urine stays dilute and she drinks to keep up.

nodes.q: Which electrocardiogram change does high calcium cause?
nodes.note: Low calcium does the opposite and lengthens the QT.

nodes.q: Which scan finds the adenoma before surgery?
nodes.note: The tracer is taken up by the overactive gland; neck ultrasound is the other localizing test. It allows a focused operation.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?
nodes.note: Offer surgery for symptoms, kidney stones, osteoporosis or fracture, calcium more than 1 mg/dL above normal, age under 50, or reduced kidney function.

nodes.q: Which drug acts on the parathyroid cell to lower PTH when surgery is not possible?
nodes.note: It makes the calcium-sensing receptor more sensitive to calcium, so the cell releases less PTH.

nodes.q: At the operation one gland is missing from its usual upper position on the right. Which embryologic event best explains this?
nodes.a: Abnormal migration of endoderm from the fourth pharyngeal pouch
nodes.note: The superior parathyroid glands come from the fourth pouch and the inferior glands (with the thymus) from the third pouch. Incomplete formation of the third pouch would remove the inferior glands and the thymus instead; failure of both pouches, as in DiGeorge syndrome, removes all glands and the thymus.

nodes.q: The brisk bleeding comes from an artery beside the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. From which artery does it arise?
nodes.a: The external carotid artery (as the superior thyroid artery)
nodes.note: The superior thyroid artery is the first branch of the external carotid and travels with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which supplies the cricothyroid muscle. The inferior thyroid artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk and runs near the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

nodes.q: Which electrolyte problem is the main risk in the days after the operation?
nodes.note: The suppressed remaining glands and a rapid uptake of calcium into hungry bone drop the calcium; treat with calcium and calcitriol.

nodes.q: Her nodule could suggest parathyroid carcinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Calcium usually above 14 mg/dL, very high PTH and a hard palpable neck mass**; invades locally
**Calcium only mildly to moderately raised (about 12) and a small nodule that cannot be felt**

nodes.note: The trap: both come from a single gland and give high calcium with high PTH.

nodes.q: Her high calcium could suggest familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low urine calcium**, lifelong mild hypercalcemia in the family, usually no symptoms; inactivating mutation of the calcium-sensing receptor; surgery does not help
**High urine calcium with kidney stones and bone disease**; no family history

nodes.q: Her calcium could be from a hidden cancer. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low PTH, weight loss, a known cancer (lung squamous cell, breast, kidney)**; PTH-related peptide or bone metastases
**High PTH, indolent course, no weight loss**

nodes.note: Both can lower phosphate and raise calcium.

nodes.q: Her aching bones could suggest multiple myeloma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Anemia, high total protein, lytic punched-out lesions, kidney failure and low PTH**
**Normal hemoglobin and protein, high PTH, thinned finger bone surfaces**

nodes.q: Her sudden back pain could suggest osteoporosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal calcium, phosphate and PTH** with a fragility fracture
**High calcium with kidney stones and subperiosteal resorption**

nodes.q: Her raised alkaline phosphatase could suggest Paget disease of bone. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Very high alkaline phosphatase with normal calcium and phosphate**; thick bones, hearing loss, mosaic bone on biopsy
**Only mildly raised alkaline phosphatase with high calcium and low phosphate**

nodes.q: Her aching bones could suggest osteomalacia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low or low-normal calcium and low phosphate** with high PTH as a response to vitamin D deficiency; Looser zones (pseudofractures) on x-ray
**High calcium**; PTH is high on its own

root.stem: A 26-year-old woman has had 6 months of headaches and trouble seeing, and milky fluid comes from both nipples when the breasts are gently pressed. Her periods were regular before, but her last period was 6 months ago. A urine pregnancy test is negative, she takes no medicines, and her thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal. Her hands, feet and jaw are unchanged. Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are low and serum prolactin is 210 ng/mL. Visual field testing shows loss of the outer half of vision in both eyes, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows a 2-cm mass in the pituitary gland.
root.oneliner: 26F + 6 months headache and poor vision + bilateral milky nipple discharge + periods stopped for 6 months + negative pregnancy test + no medicines + normal thyroid-stimulating hormone + unchanged hands, feet, jaw + low luteinizing and follicle-stimulating hormone + prolactin 210 ng/mL + loss of outer visual fields in both eyes + 2-cm pituitary mass
highlight: milky fluid comes from both nipples
Her hands, feet and jaw are unchanged
Luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are low
loss of the outer half of vision in both eyes

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A prolactin-secreting adenoma of the pituitary gland, the most common functioning pituitary tumor. The clincher: **galactorrhea + amenorrhea + very high prolactin with a pituitary mass**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: All names describe the same tumor of the prolactin-producing cells.

nodes.q: In which bony cavity does the pituitary gland sit?
nodes.a: The sella turcica (in the sphenoid bone)
nodes.note: The optic chiasm lies just above it and the cavernous sinuses at its sides.

nodes.q: Which structure does the growing mass squeeze to cause loss of the outer half of vision in both eyes?
nodes.a: The optic chiasm (crossing fibers from the nasal retinas)
nodes.note: Called bitemporal hemianopia. Macroadenomas (1 cm or more) cause headache and field loss; microadenomas (under 1 cm) cause only hormone symptoms.

nodes.q: Which hypothalamic transmitter normally holds prolactin release in check?
nodes.note: It acts on D2 receptors of the prolactin-making cells. Prolactin is the one anterior pituitary hormone under constant inhibition, so cutting the stalk or blocking dopamine raises it.

nodes.q: Why does the antiemetic metoclopramide cause galactorrhea?
nodes.a: It blocks D2 receptors, removing the dopamine brake so the anterior pituitary releases more prolactin
nodes.note: Antipsychotics act the same way.

nodes.q: Which hormone change explains why her periods stopped?
nodes.a: High prolactin suppresses gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), so luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and estrogen fall
nodes.note: In men the same mechanism lowers testosterone: less libido, impotence, testicular atrophy and sparse hair. Men often come late with large tumors and field defects.

nodes.q: Which bone problem do months of low estrogen cause in her?
nodes.note: Estrogen normally restrains osteoclasts; it recovers when prolactin is brought down.

nodes.q: Which problem can a large adenoma cause in the rest of the gland?
nodes.a: Hypopituitarism from compression of normal pituitary tissue
nodes.note: Growth hormone and the gonadotropins usually fall first.

nodes.q: In a woman of reproductive age with galactorrhea and no periods, which test comes first?
nodes.note: Then check thyroid-stimulating hormone and medicines, then image the pituitary with MRI.

nodes.q: Which drug class is first-line treatment?
nodes.note: They lower prolactin, restore periods and fertility, and shrink the tumor even when it is large. Cabergoline is usually preferred; surgery through the nose is for resistance or intolerance.

nodes.q: How do dopamine agonists lower prolactin?
nodes.a: They stimulate D2 receptors on the prolactin-making cells, mimicking dopamine
nodes.note: Side effects: nausea and orthostatic hypotension; high-dose cabergoline can cause heart valve fibrosis.

nodes.q: Her nipple discharge could suggest primary hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High thyroid-stimulating hormone with low free thyroxine**; cold intolerance, weight gain; prolactin only mildly raised because thyrotropin-releasing hormone also drives prolactin
**Normal thyroid-stimulating hormone with prolactin above 200 ng/mL and a discrete pituitary mass**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause galactorrhea and missed periods, and an underactive thyroid can enlarge the pituitary.

nodes.q: Her pituitary mass could be a non-functioning adenoma pressing on the stalk. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Prolactin only mildly raised (usually under 100 ng/mL)** because the stalk is squeezed and dopamine cannot reach the prolactin cells
**Prolactin matches the tumor size and is usually above 200 ng/mL**

nodes.q: Her bitemporal field loss could suggest craniopharyngioma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Calcified cystic suprasellar mass** from Rathke pouch remnants, in children or older adults; diabetes insipidus; prolactin only mildly raised
**Solid sellar mass without calcification and with very high prolactin**

nodes.q: Her pituitary mass could be a growth hormone adenoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Enlarging hands, feet and jaw, high insulin-like growth factor 1**, glucose intolerance, sweating
**Galactorrhea and amenorrhea with unchanged hands, feet and jaw**

nodes.note: Too little parathyroid hormone (PTH), so calcium falls. The clincher: **low calcium with high phosphate and low PTH after neck surgery, with tingling around the mouth and a facial twitch on tapping**.

nodes.q: Which event most likely caused it in him?
nodes.a: Removal of, or damage to the blood supply of, the parathyroid glands during thyroid surgery
nodes.note: The most common cause. Others: autoimmune destruction, DiGeorge syndrome (third and fourth pouch failure) and low magnesium, which blocks PTH release.

nodes.q: Which serum electrolyte abnormality explains his seizure and spasms?

nodes.q: Why does low calcium make nerves and muscles fire spontaneously?
nodes.a: Low extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for firing of nerve and muscle membranes
nodes.note: Calcium normally stabilizes sodium channels. Alkalosis from hyperventilation also lowers ionized calcium and causes lip tingling.

nodes.q: What is the facial twitch on tapping in front of the ear called?

nodes.q: Why is his phosphate high?

nodes.q: How does the loss of PTH change vitamin D metabolism?

nodes.q: Which electrocardiogram change does low calcium cause?

nodes.q: What is the acute treatment of his seizure and spasms?

nodes.q: Which long-term regimen keeps his calcium in the reference range?

nodes.q: Which brain finding on a computed tomography scan appears after years of low calcium?
nodes.note: Also cataracts and dental defects if it starts in childhood.

nodes.q: His dry skin, dry hair, aching and low mood could suggest hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

**Tingling around the mouth, carpal spasm and a Chvostek sign with low calcium**; thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal on levothyroxine

**Low PTH with high phosphate and normal 25-hydroxyvitamin D**

**Low PTH after thyroid surgery, with a normal face and normal hands**

soft spots on her skull are large

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The infant makes too little thyroid hormone from birth. The clincher: **prolonged jaundice + constipation + hoarse cry + large tongue + umbilical hernia + large fontanelles in a floppy infant**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: An old name for untreated congenital hypothyroidism; the term is now dated.

nodes.q: Which developmental problem of the thyroid is the most common cause in iodine-sufficient countries?
nodes.a: Thyroid dysgenesis (a small, absent or misplaced gland)
nodes.note: Lingual (ectopic) thyroid is the commonest form. Dyshormonogenesis is recessive and rarer; iodine deficiency is the leading cause worldwide.

nodes.q: Which process in early life depends on thyroid hormone and is permanently harmed if treatment is late?

nodes.q: Why is her jaundice prolonged?

nodes.q: Which test establishes the diagnosis?

nodes.note: The heel-prick newborn screen checks thyroid-stimulating hormone or thyroxine in the first days. Chromosome analysis, phenylalanine levels and brain imaging do not make the diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which drug treats it?
nodes.note: Start within the first 2 weeks of life and continue for life. The dose is adjusted to keep thyroid-stimulating hormone in the reference range; early treatment prevents intellectual disability.

nodes.q: Her large tongue, floppy tone and umbilical hernia could suggest Down syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Upward-slanted eyes, a single palmar crease, flat facial profile and heart defects**; trisomy 21 on karyotype
**Hoarse cry, prolonged jaundice, constipation, cool dry skin and large fontanelles** with typical eyes and hands

nodes.note: The trap: both give hypotonia, a large tongue and an umbilical hernia, and Down syndrome carries a higher risk of hypothyroidism.

nodes.q: Her lethargy and poor feeding could suggest congenital adrenal hyperplasia. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Vomiting, dehydration, low sodium, high potassium, and ambiguous genitalia in girls** (21-hydroxylase deficiency)
**Constipation, jaundice, cool skin, normal electrolytes and typical genitalia**

nodes.q: Her floppiness could suggest Tay-Sachs disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal at first, then regression at 3 to 6 months with an exaggerated startle and a cherry-red spot on the macula**; no large tongue
**Symptoms from the first weeks with a hoarse cry, large tongue and umbilical hernia; normal macula**

nodes.q: Her sleepiness and floppiness could suggest absent parathyroid glands. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low calcium with seizures and tetany, heart defects and absent thymus**
**No seizures; constipation, jaundice, large tongue and hoarse cry**

root.stem: A newborn boy, 18 hours old, is 61 cm long and weighs 5.4 kg. His mother has had poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus for 5 years. He is plethoric and jittery, and 2 hours after a serum glucose of 20 mg/dL he has a seizure. His temperature is normal, his tongue is normal in size, and there is no defect of the abdominal wall.
root.oneliner: Newborn boy, 18 hours old, + 61 cm and 5.4 kg + mother with poorly controlled type 1 diabetes for 5 years + plethoric and jittery + glucose 20 mg/dL then seizure + normal temperature + normal tongue + no abdominal wall defect
highlight: poorly controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus for 5 years
no defect of the abdominal wall

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Fetal exposure to high maternal glucose. The clincher: **a large (macrosomic) newborn with early hypoglycemia whose mother has poorly controlled diabetes**.

nodes.q: Which substance crosses the placenta from the mother and drives the fetal overgrowth?
nodes.note: Maternal insulin does not cross the placenta; glucose does, and the fetal beta cells answer with more insulin.

nodes.q: Where does the excess insulin in the newborn come from?
nodes.note: Fetal hyperinsulinism also acts as a growth factor, giving macrosomia and large organs.

nodes.q: Which pancreatic change would an autopsy show if such a newborn died after a seizure?
nodes.a: Hyperplasia of the pancreatic islet cells
nodes.note: The islets enlarge in response to the fetal hyperglycemia.

nodes.q: After the cord is clamped the glucose supply stops while insulin stays high. Which pathway, suppressed by that insulin, leaves him unable to make glucose?
nodes.note: Insulin also blocks glycogen breakdown and fat breakdown, so the hypoglycemia is worst in the first hours and can cause seizures.

nodes.q: Which blood change explains his ruddy color?
nodes.note: Fetal hyperinsulinism raises oxygen use, the fetus becomes relatively hypoxic and makes more erythropoietin. Related problems: hyperbilirubinemia, hypocalcemia and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (thick septum).

nodes.q: Which lung disease is more likely because high insulin delays surfactant production?
nodes.note: Fetal insulin blocks the cortisol-driven surfactant production by type II pneumocytes, so the lungs mature late.

nodes.q: Which birth injury is a risk because of his size?
nodes.a: Shoulder dystocia (with brachial plexus injury or clavicle fracture)
nodes.note: One reason macrosomic babies are delivered by cesarean.

nodes.q: Which lower-body malformation is the most specific for poorly controlled maternal diabetes in early pregnancy?
nodes.note: Neural tube defects and heart defects are also more frequent.

nodes.q: What is the immediate treatment for his glucose of 20 mg/dL with a seizure?
nodes.note: A bolus of 10% dextrose, then a continuous infusion with frequent glucose checks. Early feeding is enough only when he has no symptoms.

nodes.q: His large size and hypoglycemia could suggest Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Large tongue, abdominal wall defect (omphalocele) and one-sided overgrowth; mother is not diabetic**; risk of Wilms tumor
**Mother with poorly controlled diabetes, normal tongue, no abdominal wall defect**; hypoglycemia fades within days

nodes.note: The trap: both give a large newborn with fetal hyperinsulinism and hypoglycemia.

nodes.q: His jitteriness and seizure could suggest neonatal sepsis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Temperature instability, apnea, poor perfusion and an abnormal white count**; often a normal birth weight
**Macrosomia, a ruddy color and a normal temperature; the jitteriness resolves with dextrose**

root.stem: A 34-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department by her husband because she cannot see objects at the sides of her vision in either eye. She noticed it over the last day. For the past year her periods have been infrequent. She has no headache, double vision, trouble finding words, memory loss or seizures. Temperature, pulse and blood pressure are normal, and her hands, feet and face are unchanged. Visual field testing shows loss of the outer half of the visual field in both eyes. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) shows a solid 1.5-cm mass in the pituitary fossa without calcification or cysts.
root.oneliner: 34F + 1 day of lost side vision in both eyes + a year of infrequent periods + no headache, double vision, aphasia, memory loss or seizures + normal vital signs + unchanged hands, feet and face + outer visual field loss in both eyes + solid 1.5-cm pituitary mass without calcification
highlight: cannot see objects at the sides of her vision in either eye
no headache, double vision, trouble finding words, memory loss or seizures
her hands, feet and face are unchanged
loss of the outer half of the visual field in both eyes
solid 1.5-cm mass in the pituitary fossa without calcification or cysts

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A benign tumor of the anterior pituitary. The clincher: **loss of the outer half of the visual fields in both eyes (bitemporal hemianopia) from a sellar mass, with a hormone syndrome**.

nodes.q: Which structure is compressed from below to cause this field loss?
nodes.a: The optic chiasm (crossing fibers from the nasal retinas)
nodes.note: The nasal retinas see the outer (temporal) visual fields, so their crossing fibers carry the outer field of each eye.

nodes.q: Which tumor size separates a macroadenoma from a microadenoma?
nodes.note: Macroadenomas (1 cm or more) press on the chiasm; microadenomas (under 1 cm) usually give only hormone symptoms.

nodes.q: From which embryonic structure does the anterior pituitary, where this tumor arises, develop?
nodes.note: The posterior pituitary comes from neuroectoderm (a down-growth of the diencephalon). Rathke pouch remnants also give rise to craniopharyngioma.

nodes.q: Which inherited syndrome links pituitary adenomas with parathyroid and pancreatic tumors?
nodes.note: Autosomal dominant; menin is a tumor suppressor. The three Ps: pituitary, parathyroid, pancreas.

nodes.q: Her infrequent periods point to excess of which pituitary hormone?
nodes.note: Prolactinoma is the most common functioning adenoma; growth hormone and adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-secreting adenomas follow. A non-functioning macroadenoma can also raise prolactin mildly by squeezing the stalk.

nodes.q: How does that hormone make her periods infrequent?
nodes.a: It suppresses gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), so luteinizing hormone, follicle-stimulating hormone and estrogen fall
nodes.note: Galactorrhea often accompanies it.

nodes.q: Which problem can a large adenoma cause in the rest of the gland?
nodes.a: Hypopituitarism from compression of normal pituitary tissue
nodes.note: Growth hormone and the gonadotropins usually fall first, then thyroid-stimulating hormone and adrenocorticotropic hormone.

nodes.q: After the MRI, which blood test comes first?
nodes.note: Then thyroid-stimulating hormone, insulin-like growth factor 1 and a morning cortisol according to the findings.

nodes.q: How is a non-prolactin adenoma that presses on the chiasm treated?
nodes.a: Surgical removal through the nose (transsphenoidal surgery)
nodes.note: Prolactinomas are treated first with a dopamine agonist instead.

nodes.q: Her bitemporal field loss could suggest craniopharyngioma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Calcified cystic suprasellar mass** from Rathke pouch remnants, in children or older adults; diabetes insipidus
**Solid sellar mass without calcification or cysts in an adult with a hormone syndrome**

nodes.note: The trap: both are masses at the sella that press on the chiasm.

nodes.q: Her sudden loss of side vision could suggest pituitary apoplexy. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Sudden severe headache, visual loss and eye muscle palsy** from bleeding into an adenoma, with low blood pressure from acute cortisol lack
**Gradual hormone symptoms for a year, no headache and no eye muscle palsy**

nodes.q: Her mass could be a meningioma near the sella. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dural-based enhancing mass with a tail, sometimes calcified**, usually in older women; normal prolactin
**Mass arising within the pituitary fossa with infrequent periods**

nodes.q: Her vision loss could suggest optic neuritis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **One eye, painful with eye movement, central blind spot**; often multiple sclerosis
**Painless loss of the outer half of the field in both eyes**

root.stem: A 27-year-old man and his wife have been unable to conceive for 2 years. He has poor libido and cannot keep an erection. Two years ago a pituitary adenoma was removed through his nose, and since then he has taken levothyroxine and hydrocortisone. His height is normal, he has no breast enlargement, his sense of smell is normal and his testes are small and soft. Serum testosterone is very low, luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are both low, prolactin is normal, and semen analysis shows no sperm.
root.oneliner: 27M + 2 years infertility + poor libido, erectile dysfunction + pituitary adenoma removed through the nose 2 years ago on levothyroxine and hydrocortisone + normal height, no breast enlargement, normal smell + small soft testes + very low testosterone + low luteinizing and follicle-stimulating hormone + normal prolactin + no sperm
highlight: poor libido and cannot keep an erection
pituitary adenoma was removed through his nose
luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone are both low

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The testes fail because the pituitary no longer sends the signal. The clincher: **low testosterone with low (not high) luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The failure lies in the pituitary or hypothalamus, not in the testes.

nodes.q: Which pituitary cells have been lost?
nodes.a: Gonadotrophs, which make LH and FSH
nodes.note: Without LH the Leydig cells stop making testosterone; without FSH and intratesticular testosterone the Sertoli cells cannot support sperm, so he has azoospermia.

nodes.q: Which cause fits his history?
nodes.a: Damage to the pituitary by the adenoma or its removal (hypopituitarism)
nodes.note: Other causes: hyperprolactinemia, hemochromatosis, anabolic steroid use, severe illness and extreme exercise or weight loss.

nodes.q: Which inherited cause comes with a lost sense of smell?
nodes.note: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) neurons fail to migrate from the olfactory placode to the hypothalamus.

nodes.q: Which treatment restores his fertility?
nodes.a: Injections of gonadotropins (human chorionic gonadotropin, with FSH if needed)
nodes.note: Human chorionic gonadotropin acts like LH and drives testosterone production inside the testis, and FSH drives sperm production.

nodes.q: Why would testosterone patches make his sperm count worse?
nodes.a: Exogenous testosterone lowers LH and FSH through negative feedback and so lowers testosterone inside the testis
nodes.note: Patches treat low libido and low androgen effects but impair spermatogenesis.

nodes.q: Which part of the axis must still work for GnRH injections or clomiphene to help?
nodes.note: His were removed, so only gonadotropins that act directly on the testis work. GnRH pulses help hypothalamic disease such as Kallmann syndrome.

nodes.q: His small testes and infertility could suggest Klinefelter syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High LH and FSH with low testosterone, small firm testes, tall stature and gynecomastia**; 47,XXY
**Low LH and FSH, normal height and no breast enlargement**

nodes.note: The trap: both give small testes, low testosterone and azoospermia.

nodes.q: His low libido and low testosterone could suggest a prolactinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High prolactin**, headache and loss of the outer visual fields; falls with a dopamine agonist
**Normal prolactin** after the adenoma was removed

root.stem: A 30-year-old woman, pregnant for the first time, is seen at 26 weeks. She has no known diabetes, her hemoglobin A1c at the first prenatal visit was 5.2%, and her body mass index is 31 kg/m2. She has had no thirst, weight loss or ketones in the urine. A 1-hour 50-g glucose challenge gives a plasma glucose of 182 mg/dL, and a 3-hour 100-g oral glucose tolerance test shows two values above the cutoff. Ultrasound shows a fetus with an abdominal circumference above the 90th percentile and no malformations. If she receives no treatment she delivers at 40 weeks.
root.oneliner: 30F + first pregnancy at 26 weeks + no known diabetes, hemoglobin A1c 5.2% at first visit + body mass index 31 + no thirst, weight loss or ketones + 1-hour glucose challenge 182 mg/dL + 3-hour tolerance test with two abnormal values + fetal abdominal circumference above the 90th percentile, no malformations + untreated to 40 weeks
highlight: pregnant for the first time, is seen at 26 weeks
hemoglobin A1c at the first prenatal visit was 5.2%
no thirst, weight loss or ketones in the urine
abdominal circumference above the 90th percentile and no malformations

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Glucose intolerance that first appears in pregnancy. The clincher: **normal early hemoglobin A1c, then an abnormal glucose challenge and tolerance test at 24 to 28 weeks**.

nodes.q: At which weeks of pregnancy is routine screening done?
nodes.note: A 1-hour 50-g glucose challenge (positive at about 130 to 140 mg/dL) is followed by a 3-hour 100-g oral glucose tolerance test; two abnormal values make the diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which hormone made by the placenta is the main driver of insulin resistance?
nodes.note: Placental hormones (with progesterone and cortisol) rise through the third trimester, which is why the problem appears at 24 to 28 weeks in a mother whose beta cells cannot compensate.

nodes.q: Which growth problem is most likely in her baby at birth if she is not treated?
nodes.note: Maternal glucose crosses the placenta, the fetal islets make more insulin, and insulin drives fetal growth. Shoulder dystocia, neonatal hypoglycemia and respiratory distress syndrome follow.

nodes.q: Which timing explains why major malformations are not typical in her baby?
nodes.a: Her glucose rose after organogenesis, after the first trimester
nodes.note: Poorly controlled pregestational diabetes in the first trimester causes neural tube defects, sirenomelia and congenital heart disease such as ventricular septal defect.

nodes.q: What is the first step in treatment?
nodes.a: Diet and exercise, then insulin if glucose targets are missed
nodes.note: Fasting glucose goal below 95 mg/dL and 1 hour after meals below 140 mg/dL; metformin or glyburide are alternatives.

nodes.q: Why is insulin the preferred drug?
nodes.a: It does not cross the placenta
nodes.note: Most oral drugs cross to the fetus.

nodes.q: When is she retested after delivery?
nodes.a: 4 to 12 weeks after delivery, with a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test
nodes.note: The diabetes usually resolves with the placenta, but her lifetime risk of type 2 diabetes is high.

nodes.q: Her high glucose could suggest pre-existing type 2 diabetes. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hemoglobin A1c 6.5% or higher or a diabetic glucose in early pregnancy**; higher risk of malformations
**Normal early hemoglobin A1c and abnormal tests only at 24 to 28 weeks**

nodes.note: The trap: both give high glucose and a large fetus.

nodes.q: Her high glucose could suggest type 1 diabetes. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Thirst, weight loss and ketones in the urine; known since childhood or young adulthood**
**No symptoms and no ketones; first found at screening in pregnancy**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture: a pregnant woman in profile with a glucose meter and a cup of glucose drink, showing a larger-than-average fetus inside, a placenta with small hormone dots drifting to the mother's bloodstream; no text.

root.stem: A 16-year-old girl has not had a menstrual period. She is 147 cm tall (4 ft 10 in) and weighs 42 kg. Her mother says she was born with puffy hands and feet. Breast development is Tanner stage 1 and pubic hair is Tanner stage 2. She has a short, webbed neck, a broad chest, a low posterior hairline, short fourth metacarpals on both hands and multiple pigmented nevi. Blood pressure in her arms is 148/82 mm Hg and her femoral pulses are weak. A cervix is seen on pelvic examination. Serum follicle-stimulating hormone is high, and thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin are normal. Renal ultrasound shows the two kidneys joined at their lower poles.
root.oneliner: 16F + primary amenorrhea + 147 cm + puffy hands and feet at birth + no breast development, early pubic hair + short webbed neck, broad chest, low posterior hairline + short fourth metacarpals + multiple nevi + high arm blood pressure with weak femoral pulses + cervix present + high follicle-stimulating hormone + normal thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin + kidneys joined at lower poles
highlight: has not had a menstrual period
born with puffy hands and feet
thyroid-stimulating hormone and prolactin are normal
kidneys joined at their lower poles

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A disorder of the sex chromosomes in girls. The clincher: **short stature + primary amenorrhea with high follicle-stimulating hormone and a cervix present**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Exam options may write it as "gonadal dysgenesis 45,X"; also monosomy X or Ullrich-Turner syndrome.

nodes.q: Which test confirms it?
nodes.note: Shows 45,X or a mosaic such as 45,X/46,XX. If Y material is present, the gonads are removed because of the risk of gonadoblastoma.

nodes.q: Which karyotype is most common?
nodes.note: Loss of a whole X chromosome; cells have no Barr body. Partial loss (isochromosome Xq, ring X) causes the rest.

nodes.q: In which parent's gamete does the error most often happen?
nodes.a: The father's (meiotic nondisjunction in spermatogenesis, so the sperm carries no sex chromosome)
nodes.note: The single X is usually maternal. Unlike Down syndrome, Turner syndrome is **not linked to advanced maternal age**.

nodes.q: Which karyotype pattern explains milder cases, sometimes with a few spontaneous periods?
nodes.note: A mitotic nondisjunction (or X loss) after fertilization leaves two cell lines; the higher the normal line, the milder the features.

nodes.q: How many Barr bodies does a buccal smear from a 45,X girl show?
nodes.note: A Barr body is an inactivated X; with one X nothing is inactivated. 47,XXY (Klinefelter) shows one.

nodes.q: Which gene on the X chromosome, present in one copy only, explains the short stature?
nodes.note: Haploinsufficiency also gives the short fourth metacarpals and cubitus valgus.

nodes.q: What replaces her ovarian tissue?
nodes.note: Oocytes form but are lost by accelerated atresia, so the ovaries fail before puberty (primary ovarian insufficiency). Her pubic hair grows from adrenal androgens.

nodes.q: Why is her follicle-stimulating hormone high?
nodes.a: The streak ovaries make no estrogen or inhibin, so the pituitary loses negative feedback
nodes.note: Called hypergonadotropic hypogonadism (primary ovarian failure).

nodes.q: Which finding at birth reflects lymphatic obstruction in the fetus?
nodes.a: Lymphedema of the hands and feet (puffy hands and feet)
nodes.note: Fetal lymphatic channels in the neck and limbs fail to drain into the veins.

nodes.q: Which neck lesion on prenatal ultrasound comes from the same lymphatic problem and leaves her webbed neck?
nodes.note: A fluid-filled lymphatic malformation at the back of the fetal neck; large ones can cause hydrops fetalis. As it resolves it leaves the redundant skin of a webbed neck.

nodes.q: Which lesion explains her high arm blood pressure and weak femoral pulses?
nodes.note: Narrowing of the aorta just beyond the left subclavian artery (near the ductus arteriosus). Collateral flow through the intercostal arteries notches the ribs on x-ray.

nodes.q: Which heart valve anomaly is the most common in Turner syndrome?
nodes.note: It predisposes to early aortic stenosis and to aortic root dilatation.

nodes.q: Which aortic event is the leading cause of early death in women with this syndrome?
nodes.note: Bicuspid valve, coarctation, aortic dilatation and hypertension all add to the risk, and pregnancy raises it further.

nodes.q: Which kidney anomaly does her ultrasound show?
nodes.note: The fused lower poles get trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery during ascent. Other associations: Hashimoto thyroiditis, celiac disease, type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis.

nodes.q: Which hormone treatment lets her develop breasts and protects her bones?
nodes.note: Started in early adolescence. Fertility is possible only with donor eggs.

nodes.q: Which drug increases her final height?
nodes.note: Most useful when started early in childhood.

nodes.q: Her primary amenorrhea could suggest androgen insensitivity syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **46,XY with normal breasts, little or no pubic hair, no cervix or uterus (blind vagina) and testes**
**Cervix present, some pubic hair, no breast development and high follicle-stimulating hormone**

nodes.note: The trap: both present with primary amenorrhea and a normal-appearing girl.

nodes.q: Her primary amenorrhea could suggest Mullerian agenesis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal breasts, normal pubic hair, normal height and normal hormones; uterus and upper vagina absent**; 46,XX
**Cervix present, short stature, no breast development and high follicle-stimulating hormone**

nodes.q: Her lack of breast development could suggest isolated gonadotropin deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low follicle-stimulating hormone, normal height and often a lost sense of smell (Kallmann syndrome)**
**High follicle-stimulating hormone, short stature, a low hairline and short fourth metacarpals**

nodes.q: Her webbed neck and short stature could suggest Noonan syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal karyotype (46,XX or 46,XY, a RAS-pathway gene mutation), pulmonary valve stenosis**, affects boys and girls, and puberty and fertility are usually normal
**45,X with streak ovaries and high follicle-stimulating hormone, and left-sided lesions (coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve)**

image_prompts.root: Pastel teaching picture: a short, fully clothed teenage girl with a low hairline and a broad webbed neck, standing beside a simple drawing of a single X-shaped chromosome and two thin streak-like ovaries; no text.

root.stem: A 49-year-old man returns for follow-up of diabetes found 5 years ago, at age 44. He travels for work, eats fast food most days and often skips his glucose checks. He has gained 9 kg over the past 6 months and now weighs 104 kg at a height of 177 cm. He takes metformin and glyburide and reports thirst and frequent urination. His waist measures 112 cm, blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg, triglycerides are 240 mg/dL and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol is 32 mg/dL. The skin on the back of his neck and in both armpits is dark and velvety. He has no purple stretch marks or facial rounding, and his father developed diabetes at age 55. Fasting plasma glucose is 164 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c is 7.9%, urine ketones are negative, and the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is 85 mg/g (normal below 30).
root.oneliner: 49M + diabetes found at 44 + fast food, skips glucose checks + 9 kg gain in 6 months, body mass index 33 + on metformin and glyburide + thirst, frequent urination + waist 112 cm, blood pressure 146/92, high triglycerides, low HDL + dark velvety neck and armpit skin + no purple striae, no facial rounding + father diabetic at 55 + fasting glucose 164, hemoglobin A1c 7.9%, no urine ketones + albuminuria
highlight: gained 9 kg over the past 6 months
no purple stretch marks or facial rounding

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Insulin resistance with a relative lack of insulin in an overweight adult. The clincher: **obesity + acanthosis nigricans + fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL with no ketones, diagnosed in adulthood**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Non-insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus (NIDDM), or adult-onset diabetes
nodes.note: Older names for the same disease; exam options still use them.

nodes.q: Which fasting plasma glucose level, confirmed on a second day, makes the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Other criteria: hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) of 6.5% or higher, a 2-hour glucose of 200 mg/dL or more after a glucose load, or a random glucose of 200 mg/dL or more with symptoms.

nodes.q: Which defect comes first in the disease?
nodes.a: Insulin resistance (muscle, fat and liver respond poorly to insulin)
nodes.note: The pancreas first compensates with extra insulin; over years the beta cells fail, and only then does fasting glucose rise.

nodes.q: His 9-kg weight gain made his control worse. Which change in his target cells explains this?
nodes.note: Fat gain and high insulin levels lower the number of insulin receptors and weaken signaling, so less glucose transporter 4 (GLUT4) reaches the membrane of muscle and fat cells. Weight loss reverses this.

nodes.q: Which skin finding on his neck and armpits reflects his high insulin level?
nodes.note: High insulin stimulates skin cells through insulin-like growth factor receptors, which thickens and darkens the skin folds.

nodes.q: What deposits in the pancreatic islets over time?
nodes.note: Along with loss of beta cells.

nodes.q: Which enzyme turns excess glucose into sorbitol in the lens, nerves and kidney cells and is blamed for small-vessel damage?
nodes.note: Sorbitol draws water into the cells and causes swelling and injury; advanced glycation end products add to the damage.

nodes.q: Which pattern of nerve damage is the most common diabetic neuropathy?
nodes.note: Longest nerves suffer first. Loss of pain sense leads to painless foot ulcers and Charcot joints; autonomic neuropathy gives gastroparesis and orthostatic hypotension.

nodes.q: Which eye complication is the leading cause of blindness in working-age adults?
nodes.note: Seen as microaneurysms and hemorrhages, later new fragile vessels (proliferative disease).

nodes.q: How often is the eye screened?
nodes.a: A dilated eye examination at diagnosis and then every year
nodes.note: Laser or anti-vascular endothelial growth factor injections treat advanced disease.

nodes.q: His urine albumin is raised. Which kidney lesion causes it?
nodes.note: Diabetic nephropathy: the glomerular basement membrane thickens, the mesangium expands, and hyperfiltration from efferent arteriole constriction comes first. It is the leading cause of end-stage kidney disease in the US.

nodes.q: Which drug class slows the kidney damage by dilating the efferent arteriole?
nodes.a: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors (or angiotensin receptor blockers)
nodes.note: Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors block angiotensin II, so the efferent arteriole relaxes and pressure inside the glomerulus falls. They also treat his blood pressure of 146/92 mm Hg. Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors protect the kidney too, but by constricting the afferent arteriole.

nodes.q: Hyperglycemia also speeds up which large-vessel process?
Which event is the most common cause of death?
nodes.note: Often painless in diabetes because of autonomic neuropathy.

nodes.q: Which emergency of severe hyperglycemia without ketones can follow dehydration in an older patient?
nodes.note: Glucose above 600 mg/dL and very high serum osmolality. Enough insulin remains to stop ketone production, which is why ketoacidosis does not occur.

nodes.q: Which liver process does metformin inhibit to lower his glucose?
nodes.note: Metformin activates adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase. It causes no hypoglycemia and no weight gain; the rare serious adverse effect is lactic acidosis.

nodes.q: How does glyburide increase insulin release?
nodes.a: It closes adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-sensitive potassium channels in pancreatic beta cells
nodes.note: The cell depolarizes, calcium enters and insulin is released. Adverse effects are hypoglycemia and weight gain.

nodes.q: Pioglitazone is one choice for a third drug. Which receptor does it stimulate?
nodes.note: It raises insulin sensitivity in fat, muscle and liver. Adverse effects: fluid retention and heart failure, weight gain, fractures.

nodes.q: Which third-drug class prolongs the action of incretins so that beta cells release more insulin after meals?
nodes.a: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, such as sitagliptin
nodes.note: Acarbose and miglitol only block carbohydrate digestion in the gut, and pramlintide (an amylin analog) slows gastric emptying; neither releases insulin.

nodes.q: Which drug class lowers glucose by blocking its reabsorption in the proximal tubule?
nodes.a: Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, such as empagliflozin
nodes.note: Glucose spills into the urine. Adverse effects: genital yeast infections, urinary tract infections, volume loss and euglycemic ketoacidosis. They also lower heart failure and kidney events.

nodes.q: His poor control follows his travel, fast food and missed checks. What is the best next step?
nodes.a: Explore the barriers that keep him from following the diet
nodes.note: Understand the reasons first (time, cost, food knowledge); more drugs work poorly if diet is the main problem.

nodes.q: He is diabetic with thirst and frequent urination. How do you tell this from type 1 diabetes mellitus?

His skin has darkened, especially the palmar creases, the elbows and an old appendectomy scar, and there are dark patches inside his cheeks. Morning serum cortisol is 2 µg/dL, adrenocorticotropic hormone is high, sodium is 128 mEq/L, potassium is 5.6 mEq/L, glucose is 64 mg/dL and eosinophils are 9% of white cells. He has no fever, rash, cough or night sweats, no known cancer, and no headache or vision change. He has never taken steroid medicines.
