highlight: no fever, rash, cough or night sweats
normal in shape but small and shrunken

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The adrenal cortex itself fails, so cortisol and aldosterone are both lost. The clincher: **low cortisol with high adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), skin darkening and high potassium**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Chronic primary adrenal insufficiency of any cause; exam options often use this name.

nodes.q: His ACTH is high. At which level of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis is the defect?
nodes.note: Low cortisol removes negative feedback, so ACTH rises. In secondary (pituitary) or tertiary (hypothalamic) disease ACTH is low or inappropriately normal.

nodes.q: Both glands are small but normal in shape. What is the most common cause in the United States?
nodes.note: Autoantibodies against **21-hydroxylase**; T cells destroy the cortex. All three zones are lost, and the medulla is spared.

nodes.q: What does the adrenal show on biopsy or at autopsy?
nodes.a: Atrophic cortex with a lymphocytic infiltrate
nodes.note: The cortex is thin and patchy; the medulla is intact.

nodes.q: Autoimmune adrenalitis often travels with autoimmune thyroid disease and type 1 diabetes. Which syndrome is this?
nodes.note: Type 1 is the childhood form from an AIRE gene mutation: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism and adrenal insufficiency.

nodes.q: Which cause is most common worldwide?
nodes.note: Caseating granulomas destroy both glands, which look enlarged early and calcified later. Other destructive causes: disseminated fungi (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis), metastases (lung, breast), human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)-related infections and anticoagulant-related bleeding.

nodes.q: Which precursor molecule, overproduced by his pituitary, explains his darkened skin and buccal patches?
nodes.note: POMC is cleaved into ACTH, melanocyte-stimulating hormone and beta-endorphin. Melanocyte-stimulating hormone (and ACTH itself) acts on melanocortin 1 receptors on melanocytes. Secondary adrenal insufficiency has low ACTH and no darkening.

nodes.q: Which set of serum results fits: ACTH, cortisol, aldosterone, sodium and potassium?
nodes.a: High ACTH, low cortisol, low aldosterone, low sodium, high potassium
nodes.note: In the urine, sodium is high (salt wasting) and potassium is low (retained). Renin is high because the volume is low.

nodes.q: Without aldosterone, which collecting duct cells fail to secrete potassium?
nodes.note: Aldosterone opens epithelial sodium channels and potassium channels and drives the sodium-potassium pump in principal cells. Alpha-intercalated cells also secrete less acid, so a mild normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (type 4 renal tubular acidosis pattern) can appear.

nodes.q: Besides salt wasting, which hormone excess lowers his serum sodium?
nodes.note: Low volume stimulates it, and missing cortisol removes its normal restraint, so free water is kept. This is why low sodium occurs even in secondary adrenal insufficiency, where aldosterone is normal.

nodes.q: His glucose is 64 mg/dL. Which cortisol action has he lost?
nodes.note: Cortisol induces gluconeogenic enzymes (such as phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase) and frees amino acids from muscle. Low glucose is more marked in children and during fasting.

nodes.q: Which white cell change on his differential is explained by low cortisol?
nodes.note: Cortisol normally lowers eosinophils and lymphocytes and raises neutrophils; without it the pattern reverses.

nodes.q: Which test confirms that the adrenal cannot make cortisol?
nodes.note: Cortisol fails to rise after cosyntropin. A high plasma ACTH marks primary disease; a low or normal ACTH points to the pituitary or hypothalamus. Then check 21-hydroxylase antibodies, and CT the adrenals if they are negative.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening complication can follow infection, surgery or stopping steroids?
nodes.note: Vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, confusion and **shock that does not respond to fluids and vasopressors alone**; this is what kills. Low glucose, low sodium and high potassium may be present.

nodes.q: What is given at once, before test results return?
nodes.a: Intravenous hydrocortisone with normal saline (and dextrose)
nodes.note: Draw cortisol and ACTH first, but never delay treatment. High-dose hydrocortisone also covers the mineralocorticoid need.

nodes.q: Which steroid replaces the cortisol he has lost?
nodes.note: Doses are doubled or tripled during illness (sick-day rules), and an injection kit and medical alert bracelet are given.

nodes.q: Which second drug replaces the aldosterone he has lost?
nodes.note: It has strong mineralocorticoid action and corrects the salt craving, low sodium, low blood pressure and high potassium. Secondary adrenal insufficiency does not need it.

nodes.q: Suppose the same weakness followed stopping 9 months of daily prednisone for arthritis. What explains it?
nodes.a: Adrenal atrophy from suppressed ACTH secretion
nodes.note: Long-term steroids switch off corticotropin-releasing hormone and ACTH (tertiary and secondary suppression), so the zona fasciculata shrinks and cannot make cortisol for weeks after the drug stops. This is the **most common cause of adrenal insufficiency overall**. The skin stays pale and potassium is normal because the zona glomerulosa is driven by angiotensin II. Taper steroids slowly.

nodes.q: Low cortisol could come from a pituitary lesion such as Sheehan syndrome (pituitary necrosis). How do you tell them apart?

split.a: Secondary adrenal insufficiency (for example Sheehan syndrome)
split.note: **Low ACTH, no skin darkening, normal potassium**; aldosterone is preserved by angiotensin II; other pituitary hormones are often low too
**High ACTH, dark skin and buccal patches, high potassium**

nodes.note: The trap: both give weakness, low blood pressure, low sodium and low cortisol.

nodes.q: Adrenal failure can be caused by tuberculosis, metastasis, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis or fungal infection. How do you tell them apart from his disease?

split.note: **Enlarged, irregular or calcified glands, with a known primary cancer, cough or night sweats**; tuberculosis, coccidioidomycosis, lung metastases, amyloid, sarcoid
**Small glands of normal shape on both sides** and none of those features

nodes.q: Acute adrenal failure with shock could come from bleeding into both glands. How do you tell Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome from his disease?

split.note: **Sudden collapse with fever and a spreading purpuric rash in meningococcal sepsis**; endotoxin, disseminated intravascular coagulation and bilateral adrenal hemorrhage
**Months of weakness and darkening skin without fever or rash**

nodes.note: Waterhouse-Friderichsen is acute primary adrenal insufficiency, so there is no time for skin darkening. Classic in children with Neisseria meningitidis.

nodes.q: An adrenal tumor such as adrenocortical carcinoma could also be on the list. How do you tell it from his disease?

split.note: **A large one-sided adrenal mass that makes too much hormone** (Cushing syndrome, virilization); the other gland is suppressed but the patient is not cortisol deficient
**Both glands small and symmetric with hormone deficiency**

nodes.q: Pituitary disease could also change cortisol. How do you tell Cushing disease (a basophilic pituitary adenoma) apart?

split.note: **High cortisol and high ACTH with high blood pressure, weight gain and purple striae**
**Low cortisol with low blood pressure and weight loss**; ACTH is high for the opposite reason

nodes.note: Both have a high ACTH, but cortisol moves in opposite directions.

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Exogenous thyrotoxicosis (too much thyroid hormone medicine)
nodes.note: Thyroid hormone excess from an outside source. The clincher: **hyperthyroid symptoms in a patient taking thyroid hormone, with suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and low radioactive iodine uptake**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The term factitia is used when the hormone is taken secretly, but the hormonal pattern is the same.

nodes.q: Which results fit: free thyroxine, free triiodothyronine and radioactive iodine uptake?
nodes.a: Free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine increased, radioactive iodine uptake decreased
nodes.note: High hormone levels switch off TSH, so the thyroid gland is idle and takes up little iodine.

nodes.q: Suppose she took liothyronine (triiodothyronine) instead. What would her free thyroxine be?
nodes.note: Liothyronine adds only triiodothyronine, so free triiodothyronine rises while free thyroxine falls. With an intact gland, the suppressed TSH also stops it making thyroxine. TSH is low either way.

nodes.q: Which receptor change explains her fast pulse and tremor?
nodes.a: More beta-1 adrenergic receptors (thyroid hormone upregulates them)
nodes.note: The heart becomes more sensitive to catecholamines. This is why propranolol eases symptoms; it also slightly blocks peripheral conversion of thyroxine to triiodothyronine.

nodes.q: Which blood marker is low in this disease and high in thyroiditis?
nodes.note: It comes only from thyroid tissue, which is idle here.

nodes.q: What is the most appropriate treatment?
nodes.note: Propranolol can ease palpitations and tremor in the meantime. Recheck TSH after about 6 to 8 weeks.

nodes.q: Which rhythm disturbance can long-term excess cause?
nodes.note: Long-term excess also thins bone (osteoporosis). Over-replacement is common in older patients; keep TSH in range.

nodes.q: Palpitations, tremor and a low TSH could suggest Graves disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Diffuse goiter, eye disease, high radioactive iodine uptake and thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins**; no hormone medicine
**Thyroid hormone medicine, no goiter or eye signs, low iodine uptake**

nodes.note: The trap: both give high thyroid hormones and a low TSH.

nodes.q: A hot thyroid nodule can also give a low TSH. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Palpable single nodule with focal high iodine uptake** and a quiet rest of the gland
**No nodule and low uptake throughout**; she has had a thyroidectomy

nodes.q: Nervousness and insomnia could suggest an anxiety disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal thyroid-stimulating hormone and free thyroxine**; no hormone excess
**TSH 0.1 µU/mL with high free thyroxine and brisk reflexes**

type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, high cholesterol
pain in both knees and hips
blocks fat absorption in the gut

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Excess body fat that harms health. The clincher: **body mass index (BMI) of 30 kg/m2 or more**; hers is about 37.

nodes.q: Which BMI range defines overweight?
nodes.note: Obesity is 30 or more; class 3 obesity is 40 or more.

nodes.q: Which joint disease do her knees and hips suggest?
nodes.note: Extra weight overloads the joints. Other complications include sleep apnea, fatty liver, gallstones and cancers such as endometrial cancer.

nodes.q: Which satiety hormone from her fat cells is high, yet fails to curb her appetite?
nodes.note: Leptin acts on the arcuate nucleus of the hypothalamus to cut hunger; common obesity shows leptin resistance. Ghrelin from the stomach does the opposite and rises before meals. Rare leptin or leptin-receptor mutations cause severe childhood obesity.

nodes.q: What is the first treatment for everyone?

nodes.q: Which enzymes does the fat-blocking drug inhibit?

nodes.q: Which problem is she most likely to have in the first month?

nodes.q: Which older weight-loss drug raised blood pressure and heart rate and was withdrawn?

nodes.q: Her weight, blood pressure and glucose could suggest the metabolic syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

highlight: her breasts have produced no milk

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: The enlarged pregnant pituitary has a fragile blood supply and infarcts when blood pressure falls after a hemorrhage. The clincher: **no milk and fatigue after a delivery complicated by bleeding and hypotension**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Exam options may list it as "pituitary necrosis". It is infarction of the anterior pituitary after a delivery with heavy bleeding.

nodes.q: Why is the pituitary vulnerable in pregnancy?
nodes.a: Lactotroph hyperplasia enlarges the gland, but its blood supply does not keep up
nodes.note: The low-pressure portal vessels are the first to fail when blood pressure drops.

nodes.q: Which set of results fits: adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), thyroid-stimulating hormone, prolactin and aldosterone?

nodes.q: Why is her aldosterone preserved, unlike in primary adrenal failure?

nodes.q: Which test shows the pituitary?

nodes.q: Which replacement is started first?

nodes.q: Fatigue and orthostasis could suggest primary adrenal insufficiency. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.note: The trap: both give low cortisol, fatigue and low blood pressure.

nodes.q: Fatigue could suggest primary hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High thyroid-stimulating hormone with low thyroxine**; milk production and periods preserved
**Low thyroid-stimulating hormone with low thyroxine, and no milk**

nodes.q: Lethargy after delivery could suggest postpartum depression. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low mood or loss of interest** with normal hormones and normal milk production
**Failure to lactate, orthostasis, low pituitary hormones**

nodes.q: A pituitary problem after delivery could suggest lymphocytic hypophysitis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Headache and an enlarged pituitary on imaging**, with no severe hemorrhage at delivery
**Delivery with hemorrhage and hypotension, then an empty or small sella**

no bulging eyes and no palpitations

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Autoimmune destruction of the thyroid and the most common cause of hypothyroidism where iodine intake is adequate (iodine deficiency leads worldwide). The clincher: **painless firm goiter + hypothyroidism + lymphocytes with lymphoid follicles on biopsy**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Same disease.

nodes.q: Which antibody is the most sensitive marker?
nodes.note: Anti-thyroglobulin antibodies are also common but less sensitive.

nodes.q: Which immune mechanism destroys the thyroid?
nodes.a: Cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity by cytotoxic T cells
nodes.note: Antibody-dependent killing (type II) adds to the damage. It is linked to human leukocyte antigen (HLA)-DR3 and DR5 and to other autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes.

nodes.q: Which altered follicular cell is also characteristic on the biopsy?
nodes.note: Large cells with pink, granular cytoplasm packed with mitochondria. The lymphoid follicles have germinal centers; follicle destruction and fibrosis follow.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?

nodes.q: Which thyroid cancer carries an increased risk in this disease?

nodes.q: Which short transient phase can occur early, before the thyroid fails?

**Hypothyroidism, firm nodular goiter, lymphocytes with follicles**

nodes.q: A goiter could suggest viral (subacute granulomatous) thyroiditis. How do you tell them apart?

**Diffuse firm nodular gland with lymphoid follicles**

**Hypothyroidism with diffuse enlargement**

nodes.q: What are the three parts of Whipple triad?

nodes.q: Which of his two drugs releases his own insulin regardless of the glucose level?

nodes.q: Which counterregulatory hormone is the first-line defense as glucose falls?

nodes.q: Cortisol from the adrenal cortex induces which enzyme in the adrenal medulla?

nodes.q: Which symptoms are caused by epinephrine release?
nodes.note: Confusion is neuroglycopenic: the brain lacks glucose.

nodes.q: Which antihypertensive drug class can mask these warning symptoms?
nodes.note: They blunt tremor and palpitations; sweating is spared because sweat glands are driven by sympathetic cholinergic fibers. Repeated episodes also cause hypoglycemia unawareness.

nodes.q: What is the immediate treatment for a patient who can swallow?

nodes.note: Give intravenous dextrose if he cannot swallow, or intramuscular glucagon if no intravenous access. Recheck in 15 minutes.

nodes.q: If an unexplained episode occurs, which test separates insulin injection from sulfonylurea or insulinoma?
nodes.note: High insulin with a low C-peptide means injected insulin; high insulin with a high C-peptide means a sulfonylurea or insulinoma.

nodes.q: Low glucose after a fast could suggest an insulinoma. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.note: The trap: both give high insulin during episodes.

nodes.q: Low glucose, weakness and sweating could suggest adrenal insufficiency. How do you tell them apart?

nodes.q: Before giving erythropoietin, which iron measurements are checked?

root.stem: A 12-year-old boy has had 3 weeks of frequent urination, constant thirst, tiredness and a 3-kg weight loss. He is thin, and the rest of his physical examination is normal. His fasting blood glucose is 350 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows 4+ glucose.
root.oneliner: 12M + 3 weeks of frequent urination, constant thirst, tiredness + 3-kg weight loss + thin + fasting glucose 350 mg/dL + 4+ glucose in the urine

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Autoimmune destruction of the pancreatic beta cells leaves the body with almost no insulin. The clincher: **a thin child with polyuria, polydipsia and weight loss, a fasting glucose above 126 mg/dL and glucose in the urine**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, also called juvenile-onset diabetes
nodes.note: Both are older names for the same disease.

nodes.q: What destroys the insulin-producing cells?
nodes.a: An autoimmune attack by T cells on the pancreatic beta cells
nodes.note: Lymphocytes infiltrate the islets (insulitis). Antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase, insulin and islet cells may be present. Symptoms appear only after most of the beta cells are gone.

nodes.q: Which human leukocyte antigen (HLA) types carry the inherited risk?
nodes.note: HLA class II genes present antigen to helper T cells. Type 2 diabetes has a stronger family link but no HLA association.

nodes.q: Why does glucose spill into his urine when the kidney normally reclaims all of it?
nodes.a: The filtered glucose load exceeds the transport maximum, so the sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT-1 and SGLT-2) of the proximal tubule are saturated
nodes.note: Glucose appears in the urine once blood glucose passes about 180 mg/dL. The glucose left in the tubule holds water with it (osmotic diuresis), which explains the frequent urination and thirst. The glucose carriers on the blood side of the cell (glucose transporter 2) are not the limit.

nodes.q: Insulin moves glucose into skeletal muscle and fat by placing which transporter in the cell membrane?
nodes.note: Without insulin, muscle and fat cannot take up glucose, so blood glucose rises even as the cells starve. Brain, red cells, liver and beta cells use insulin-independent transporters (GLUT1, GLUT2, GLUT3).

nodes.q: Which life-threatening acute complication develops when insulin is missing or too low during an illness?
nodes.note: Without insulin, fat is broken down and the liver makes acids called ketones.

nodes.q: In untreated disease the body overproduces ketone bodies, as it does in prolonged starvation. Which factor do the two states share?
nodes.a: Increased availability of acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) from fatty acid oxidation
nodes.note: Low insulin effect (or a low insulin-to-glucagon ratio) releases fatty acids from fat, and the liver burns them to acetyl-CoA. Oxaloacetate is used up making glucose, so the acetyl-CoA is turned into ketone bodies. Fatty acid oxidation and gluconeogenesis are increased, not inhibited.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Lifelong subcutaneous insulin: a long-acting basal dose plus short-acting doses at meals
nodes.note: Mealtime doses are matched to the carbohydrate eaten. A pump or continuous glucose monitor can be used.

nodes.q: A 4-year-old girl with the disease has restlessness, sweating and confusion during the night, 6 hours after her father raised both her intermediate-acting and long-acting insulin doses at bedtime following a day of sweets. Her fingerstick glucose the next morning is 72 mg/dL and her urine has no glucose or ketones. What most likely explains the night?
nodes.a: Hypoglycemia from too much insulin, which resolved by itself
nodes.note: Sweating and restlessness come from the adrenergic (autonomic) response, and confusion from the brain's lack of glucose (neuroglycopenia). For a single big meal only the short-acting insulin is adjusted; the basal dose is left alone.

nodes.q: A boy on insulin becomes tremulous one hour after his morning dose, and his glucose is later higher than before. What is this rebound called?
nodes.note: Hypoglycemia triggers glucagon, epinephrine, then cortisol and growth hormone, so glucose overshoots. Classically the low comes at night and the rebound high is seen in the morning. The dawn phenomenon differs: a morning rise from growth hormone and cortisol with no preceding low.

nodes.q: Glucagon and epinephrine raise blood glucose in the liver by activating which enzyme?
nodes.a: Adenylyl cyclase (raising cyclic adenosine monophosphate and protein kinase A, which switch on glycogen breakdown)
nodes.note: Glucagon acts through a stimulatory G protein (Gs); the rise in cyclic adenosine monophosphate activates protein kinase A, which turns on glycogen phosphorylase and turns off glycogen synthase. Muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose because muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase.

nodes.q: After years of repeated lows, a woman with the disease faints without her old sweating, fast pulse and shaking. What is this loss called?
nodes.a: Hypoglycemia unawareness (loss of the adrenergic warning symptoms)
nodes.note: Repeated hypoglycemia blunts the epinephrine response, and autonomic neuropathy adds to it. Keeping glucose a little higher for a few weeks can restore the warning symptoms.

nodes.q: She is found unconscious during an episode. An injected drug helps by which mechanism?
nodes.a: Stimulating hepatic glucose production (glucagon drives glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis in the liver)
nodes.note: Intravenous dextrose is the alternative when a line is in place. Nothing is given by mouth to an unconscious patient. Glucagon fails when liver glycogen is depleted.

nodes.q: A 13-year-old girl with a 6-year history of the disease has had poor control for 2 months. She takes her insulin but struggles with her diet, and her parents argue with each other and with her at meals. What is the most appropriate next step?
nodes.a: Discuss further the impact of her illness on the family
nodes.note: Diabetes affects the whole family, so explore the stress before advising, referring or blaming. Telling the parents to stop bickering is judgmental; psychotherapy and dietician referral come after the family problem is understood.

nodes.q: A 16-year-old boy diagnosed 6 months ago has poor control, and you suspect he is reluctant to inject himself. Which way of raising the issue is best?
nodes.a: An open-ended, empathic question such as "Giving yourself insulin injections can be difficult. What's it like for you?"
nodes.note: Open questions invite him to talk. Labels ("poorly controlled"), closed questions about missed shots and quick offers of help close the conversation.

nodes.q: A 17-year-old girl with repeated admissions for ketoacidosis and a hemoglobin A1c of 11.5% says she forgets her insulin or is too busy. What is the best first step?
nodes.a: Acknowledge her reasons for missing insulin injections
nodes.note: Validating her view builds trust. Lecturing about complications, going to her parents or referring her comes after that.

nodes.q: Which other autoimmune diseases should be looked for at diagnosis and then periodically?
nodes.a: Autoimmune thyroid disease and celiac disease
nodes.note: Check thyroid-stimulating hormone and anti-tissue transglutaminase antibodies. Eye, urine albumin and foot screening begin after several years of disease.

nodes.q: After years of poor control, which kidney lesion appears?
nodes.a: Diabetic nephropathy: glomerular basement membrane thickening and mesangial expansion, with Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules
nodes.note: Hyperfiltration comes first; moderately increased albuminuria (microalbuminuria) is the first measurable sign. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors slow progression.

nodes.q: His high glucose could suggest type 2 diabetes, which now occurs in children too. How do you tell the two apart?

split.note: Usually **obese, acanthosis nigricans, insulin resistance with a high C-peptide**; slow onset, ketosis uncommon at first
**Thin child with weeks of polyuria and weight loss, low or absent C-peptide, autoantibodies and a tendency to ketosis**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a high glucose and glucose in the urine.

nodes.q: Frequent urination in a child has other causes. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Glucose in the urine with a normal blood glucose**
**Large volumes of dilute urine with a normal blood glucose**
Glucose in the urine and a high blood glucose
**Excess water drinking with dilute urine and a low-normal sodium**
Weight loss, high glucose and glucose in the urine

nodes.note: Only one of them has a high blood glucose.

root.stem: A 16-year-old boy with type 1 diabetes, usually well controlled, is brought to the emergency department with 6 hours of vomiting and abdominal pain. He has had a fever and a productive cough for 3 days. He is drowsy and breathing deeply and rapidly, and his breath smells fruity. His pulse is 124/min and his blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg; his skin turgor is poor. Glucose is 612 mg/dL, sodium 134 mEq/L, chloride 96 mEq/L, potassium 5.9 mEq/L, bicarbonate 7 mEq/L and arterial pH 7.10, and the urine contains large amounts of ketones.
root.oneliner: 16M + type 1 diabetes, usually well controlled + 3 days of fever and productive cough + vomiting, abdominal pain + drowsy + deep rapid breathing, fruity breath + pulse 124, BP 88/54, poor skin turgor + glucose 612, Na 134, Cl 96, K 5.9, bicarbonate 7, pH 7.10 + large urine ketones
highlight: fever and a productive cough for 3 days

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A complication of absolute insulin deficiency. The clincher: **high glucose + ketones in blood or urine + metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.3, bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L) with deep rapid breathing and fruity breath**.

nodes.q: Which event most likely tipped this usually well-controlled patient into ketoacidosis?
nodes.note: Infection raises the insulin requirement through stress hormones (epinephrine, cortisol, glucagon). Other triggers are missed insulin, a first presentation of the disease, myocardial infarction and some drugs.

nodes.q: Which hormone state drives the disease?
nodes.a: Severe insulin deficiency with excess glucagon and other counter-regulatory hormones
nodes.note: Fat tissue breaks down into free fatty acids, and the liver turns them into acetyl coenzyme A and then into ketones. Glucose is also made and not used.

nodes.q: Which compounds pile up in his blood from this fat breakdown?
nodes.a: Ketone bodies (mostly beta-hydroxybutyrate, with acetoacetate), along with free fatty acids
nodes.note: Acetone is made from acetoacetate and gives the fruity breath. The nitroprusside urine test detects acetoacetate but not beta-hydroxybutyrate, so it can understate the severity. Ammonia and carnitine are not the problem.

nodes.q: Which acid-base disorder do the ketones cause?
nodes.note: Anion gap = sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate) = 134 - (96 + 7) = 31 mEq/L (normal about 8 to 12), because beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate are unmeasured anions.

nodes.q: What is his deep, rapid breathing called?
nodes.note: It blows off carbon dioxide to raise the pH: the lungs compensating for the metabolic acidosis, so arterial carbon dioxide pressure is low.

nodes.q: Why is he so volume-depleted?
nodes.a: Osmotic diuresis from the glucose in the urine, worsened by vomiting
nodes.note: He can lose several liters of water along with sodium and potassium. The measured sodium looks low because high glucose pulls water out of cells.

nodes.q: Which change best explains his drowsiness?
nodes.a: Intracellular and extracellular dehydration from a very high plasma osmolality, with acidosis
nodes.note: Brain cells still take up glucose without insulin and can still do glycolysis. The problem is shrunken cells and acidosis, not a lack of glucose transport or fatty acids in the spinal fluid.

nodes.q: His serum potassium is high although his total body potassium is low. Why?
nodes.a: Potassium moves out of cells because of insulin deficiency, acidosis and high osmolality
nodes.note: Urinary losses from osmotic diuresis drain the body's stores.

nodes.q: What happens to his serum potassium once insulin and saline are given?
nodes.a: It falls, because insulin drives potassium back into cells
nodes.note: Insulin activates the sodium-potassium pump and cells take potassium up; urine losses continue.

nodes.q: If a comatose patient with this disease arrives with a potassium of only 3 mEq/L and insulin is started without potassium, which event can follow?
nodes.a: Fatal ventricular arrhythmia with cardiac arrest from severe hypokalemia
nodes.note: Insulin pushes the little potassium left into cells, and the low potassium triggers the arrhythmia. Potassium must be replaced first when it is below 3.3 mEq/L, and added to the fluids once it is below about 5.2 mEq/L.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Isotonic saline first, then a continuous intravenous insulin infusion, with potassium replaced as needed
nodes.note: Fluids come before insulin. Add dextrose once glucose falls to about 200 to 250 mg/dL so insulin can keep running to clear the ketones. Bicarbonate is given only for a pH below 6.9.

nodes.q: Four hours into treatment, which pattern of laboratory changes is expected?
nodes.a: Potassium down, bicarbonate up, urea nitrogen down, pH up and arterial carbon dioxide pressure up
nodes.note: Saline restores volume, so urea nitrogen falls. Ketone production stops, so bicarbonate and pH rise, and the lungs no longer need to blow off carbon dioxide.

nodes.q: Insulin switches off glucose output and storage breakdown in the liver. Which hepatic enzyme becomes more active?
nodes.note: Insulin induces glucokinase, trapping glucose in the liver cell. Glucose-6-phosphatase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase, glycogen phosphorylase and phosphorylase kinase are all turned down.

nodes.q: Which measure shows that the ketoacidosis has resolved?
nodes.note: Glucose often normalizes first; stopping insulin early lets ketosis return.

nodes.q: Hours after treatment begins, a child develops a headache, vomiting and falling consciousness. Which complication is this?
nodes.note: It is most feared in children and is linked to a rapid fall in plasma osmolality; treat with mannitol or hypertonic saline.

nodes.q: Days into another admission for ketoacidosis, a 45-year-old woman develops facial pain, swelling around one eye and a black crust on the nasal turbinate. Which infection is this?
nodes.note: Acidosis and high glucose (and free iron) let the fungus grow. It invades blood vessels, causing tissue death, and spreads from the sinuses to the orbit and brain (cavernous sinus thrombosis), which kills. Biopsy shows broad, ribbon-like hyphae with few septa branching at wide angles.

nodes.q: Which treatment is needed besides correcting the ketoacidosis?
nodes.a: Urgent surgical debridement plus intravenous amphotericin B
nodes.note: Delay is often fatal; the disease spreads to the brain within days.

nodes.q: His very high glucose and dehydration could suggest a hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Older adult with **type 2 diabetes, glucose above 600 mg/dL, serum osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg and little or no ketosis**; confusion and coma develop over days
**Type 1 diabetes, glucose usually above 250 mg/dL, ketones, pH below 7.3 and Kussmaul breathing**; develops over hours to a day

nodes.note: The trap: both produce profound dehydration and altered mental status.

nodes.q: Other causes of a gap acidosis were also possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Binge drinking then vomiting, low or normal glucose**
Alcohol use and a normal glucose
**Prolonged fasting with mild acidosis and a normal glucose**
Severe acidosis and glucose of 612 mg/dL
**Shock, sepsis or metformin with high lactate and no ketones**
**Tinnitus, early respiratory alkalosis then metabolic acidosis, normal glucose**
Tinnitus or aspirin ingestion, and a normal glucose

nodes.note: Only diabetic ketoacidosis combines glucose, ketones and acidosis.

root.stem: A 13-year-old boy is teased at school for "having breasts like a girl". He has had no illnesses and takes no medicines. He is at the 50th percentile for height and the 60th percentile for weight and body mass index. Examination shows bilateral, 1-cm, mildly tender, rubbery nodules under the areolae. His genital development is Tanner stage 3, and the testes feel normal. There is no nipple discharge.
root.oneliner: 13M + teased for breasts + healthy, no medicines + height 50th, BMI 60th percentile + bilateral 1-cm tender rubbery subareolar nodules + Tanner 3, normal testes + no nipple discharge
highlight: no illnesses and takes no medicines

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A benign, self-limited growth of breast gland tissue in boys in mid-puberty. The clincher: **bilateral small tender rubbery subareolar nodules in an otherwise healthy boy at Tanner stage 3 with normal growth and normal testes**.

nodes.q: Which hormone imbalance causes it?
nodes.note: Estradiol rises ahead of testosterone early in puberty. Aromatase also converts testosterone to estradiol in fat and other tissues.

nodes.q: A 32-year-old man with hypopituitarism develops swollen, tender breasts after starting human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) injections. Where does hCG act to cause this?
nodes.a: The testis: it mimics luteinizing hormone and raises testicular estradiol production
nodes.note: The excess estradiol, relative to testosterone, stimulates the breast gland. hCG does not act on the breast directly.

nodes.q: A 55-year-old man with alcoholic cirrhosis develops the same breast swelling. Why does liver failure tip the balance?
nodes.a: The damaged liver clears less estrogen and its precursors, so more androstenedione is converted to estrogen by aromatase in fat
nodes.note: Sex hormone-binding globulin also rises and binds testosterone more tightly than estradiol, lowering free testosterone. Spider angiomas and palmar erythema have the same cause.

nodes.q: He is worried that the swelling means something is wrong. How common is this at his stage of puberty?
nodes.a: Very common: up to about half to two-thirds of boys have it in mid-puberty (around 13 to 14 years, Tanner 3 to 4)
nodes.note: It is not typical at 9 to 10 years, before puberty; breast growth before puberty needs a work-up.

nodes.q: Which potassium-sparing diuretic that blocks the androgen receptor is a classic drug cause?
nodes.note: Spironolactone blocks the androgen receptor and raises estrogen activity. Others: ketoconazole (blocks androgen synthesis), cimetidine, digoxin, alcohol, marijuana, anabolic steroids, finasteride and androgen-deprivation drugs for prostate cancer.

nodes.q: What is the most appropriate next step in management?
nodes.a: Reassurance and follow-up, with no laboratory tests or imaging
nodes.note: The history and examination are typical. No hormone levels, no mammography; plot growth and Tanner stage at follow-up.

nodes.q: After empathizing with this embarrassed boy, what should you tell him about the outlook?
nodes.a: It usually goes away by itself within about 12 to 18 months
nodes.note: Most cases settle within 1 to 2 years. Do not tell him that nobody notices; acknowledge his feelings.

nodes.q: Which treatment is considered if it persists for years or causes great distress?
nodes.a: Surgical removal of the breast tissue
nodes.note: Referral is also appropriate for a mass larger than 4 cm. Tamoxifen is sometimes tried.

nodes.q: His enlarged breasts could suggest Klinefelter syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small firm testes, tall eunuchoid build, low testosterone with high follicle-stimulating and luteinizing hormones, 47,XXY**; infertility and learning problems
**Normal testes, normal height and weight percentiles, normal pubertal progress**; nothing else abnormal

nodes.note: The trap: both give bilateral gynecomastia in a teenager.

nodes.q: Other causes of a swollen breast were also possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Galactorrhea, headache, visual field defect, high prolactin**
**Painless hard testicular mass; hCG-secreting germ cell or estrogen-secreting Leydig cell tumor**
**Unilateral hard, fixed, eccentric mass or bloody discharge; very rare in boys**
A hard mass or discharge; mammography is not needed
**Soft fatty enlargement in an obese boy with no firm disc under the nipple**

nodes.note: Each has a feature missing from his case.

root.stem: A 29-year-old woman has had nervousness, tremor, palpitations and heat intolerance for 3 weeks, starting 6 weeks after she delivered a healthy baby. She has lost 5 kg. Her pulse is 104/min. The thyroid gland is firm, about twice normal size and not tender. She has no neck pain, no fever, no bulging eyes and no skin changes on the shins. Her thyroid-stimulating hormone is below 0.03 µU/mL, free thyroxine is high, and 24-hour radioactive iodine uptake is 1% (normal 8% to 25%).
root.oneliner: 29F + nervousness, tremor, palpitations, heat intolerance, 5-kg weight loss starting 6 weeks after delivery + firm painless goiter twice normal size + no neck pain, fever, bulging eyes or shin skin changes + suppressed TSH, high free T4, radioiodine uptake 1%
highlight: 6 weeks after she delivered a healthy baby
firm, about twice normal size and not tender
no skin changes on the shins

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A painless, autoimmune lymphocytic thyroiditis that arises within a year of delivery. The clincher: **thyrotoxicosis after delivery with a painless firm goiter, suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone, high free thyroxine and a very low radioactive iodine uptake**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Painless (silent) thyroiditis, also called subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis
nodes.note: Postpartum thyroiditis is the form of painless lymphocytic thyroiditis that follows pregnancy; exam options may use either name.

nodes.q: What happens inside the gland?
nodes.a: Lymphocytes infiltrate and damage the follicular cells, which leak stored thyroid hormone
nodes.note: The thyrotoxicosis comes from release of preformed hormone, not from new production.

nodes.q: Why is the radioactive iodine uptake only 1% in a woman with a high thyroid hormone level?
nodes.a: The hormone is leaking from damaged follicles, not newly made, and the suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone shuts off iodine uptake
nodes.note: Uptake is high in Graves disease, where the gland overproduces hormone.

nodes.q: Which antibody is often present, and marks a higher risk of later hypothyroidism?
nodes.note: The same antibody is found in Hashimoto thyroiditis.

nodes.q: What is the usual sequence of thyroid function?
nodes.a: A thyrotoxic phase, then a hypothyroid phase, then recovery to normal
nodes.note: Thyrotoxicosis lasts 1 to 3 months and hypothyroidism several months; most women recover.

nodes.q: Which long-term outcome do a fraction of these women face?
nodes.note: About a fifth to a third of women stay hypothyroid, more often those with high anti-thyroid peroxidase antibodies. It tends to recur after later pregnancies. Check thyroid-stimulating hormone yearly.

nodes.q: What treatment relieves her symptoms in the thyrotoxic phase?
nodes.note: Antithyroid drugs do not work because the gland is not overproducing hormone. Levothyroxine is given only if the hypothyroid phase is symptomatic.

nodes.q: Her tremor, weight loss and goiter could suggest Graves disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Diffuse goiter + bulging eyes or shin skin changes + high radioactive iodine uptake + stimulating thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies**
**Painless firm goiter after delivery with a radioactive iodine uptake of 1%**; no eye or skin signs

nodes.note: The trap: both give high thyroid hormone and low thyroid-stimulating hormone after pregnancy.

nodes.q: A swollen thyroid with high thyroid hormone could suggest subacute granulomatous thyroiditis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Painful, tender thyroid after a viral illness, with fever and a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate**; low uptake
**Painless, nontender goiter after delivery without fever**

nodes.q: Her low iodine uptake could also suggest a new mother secretly taking thyroid hormone pills. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small or normal-size gland with a low serum thyroglobulin**; low uptake; often a health worker or someone trying to lose weight
**Enlarged firm gland after delivery with a high serum thyroglobulin** from the damaged follicles; low uptake

nodes.note: Both give thyrotoxicosis with a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone and a low uptake; thyroglobulin separates them.

nodes.q: Other thyroid conditions were also possible. Which finding in her case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: **Single hot nodule with high focal uptake**
A single nodule and high uptake
**Goiter with anti-peroxidase antibodies, usually hypothyroid, not thyrotoxic**
A hypothyroid picture; she is thyrotoxic
**Rapidly growing hard fixed neck mass in an elderly patient**
Old age and a hard, fast-growing mass
**Rapid enlargement in a patient with long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis**
Rapid growth on a background of long-standing Hashimoto thyroiditis

nodes.note: None of them gives thyrotoxicosis with a painless goiter and a 1% uptake soon after delivery.

root.stem: A 35-year-old woman has had 1 year of fatigue, lethargy, a 9-kg weight gain and constant coldness. Her skin is coarse, and the relaxation phase of the Achilles reflex is delayed. No thyroid tissue can be felt in the neck, and no cystic neck mass moves with swallowing. A small smooth swelling is seen at the base of her tongue behind a tiny midline pit. Thyroxine and triiodothyronine are low, and thyroid-stimulating hormone is high. A radioactive iodine scan shows uptake in the midline at the back of the tongue and none in the neck.
root.oneliner: 35F + 1 year of fatigue, 9-kg weight gain, cold intolerance + coarse skin, delayed Achilles relaxation + no thyroid felt in the neck, no mobile neck mass + swelling at tongue base behind a midline pit + low thyroxine and triiodothyronine, high thyroid-stimulating hormone + radioiodine uptake at tongue base, none in the neck
highlight: relaxation phase of the Achilles reflex is delayed
No thyroid tissue can be felt in the neck
no cystic neck mass moves with swallowing
uptake in the midline at the back of the tongue and none in the neck

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Ectopic thyroid tissue at the base of the tongue, the most common site of ectopic thyroid, and often the patient's only thyroid tissue. The clincher: **radioactive iodine taken up at the midline base of the tongue and none in the neck, with hypothyroidism**.

nodes.q: Which embryologic failure explains it?
nodes.a: The thyroid failed to descend along the thyroglossal duct from the back of the tongue to the neck
nodes.note: The thyroid begins at the foramen cecum on the back of the tongue and descends along the thyroglossal duct, in front of the hyoid bone and larynx, to the front of the neck by about week 7.

nodes.q: Which landmark is the midline pit at the back of the tongue where the thyroid began?
nodes.note: It sits at the apex of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis, where the anterior two-thirds and posterior third of the tongue meet. The radioactive iodine lies just behind and below (inferior to) it.

nodes.q: Why is she hypothyroid?
nodes.a: The small ectopic gland cannot make enough thyroid hormone for the body
nodes.note: It is usually her only thyroid tissue, so the high thyroid-stimulating hormone cannot drive enough output.

nodes.q: The mass may grow when demand for thyroid hormone rises, as in puberty or pregnancy. Which structure is it most likely to obstruct?
nodes.a: The upper airway (with trouble swallowing and a muffled voice)
nodes.note: Its spot at the tongue base, just above the epiglottis, explains the symptoms. Shrinking it with levothyroxine is the first step.

nodes.q: Thyroid hormone acts on target cells through which kind of receptor?
nodes.a: Nuclear receptors (thyroid hormone receptor bound to retinoid X receptor) that switch on gene transcription
nodes.note: Mainly triiodothyronine enters the cell and binds the receptor in the nucleus, which drops corepressors and recruits coactivators. Effects include brain development, metabolic rate, beta-adrenergic receptor expression, bone growth and heart function.

nodes.q: A newborn has a mass at the base of the tongue and no thyroid in the neck. Which thyroid disorder must be looked for?
nodes.note: Thyroid dysgenesis (ectopic, absent or small gland) is the most common cause of congenital hypothyroidism. Newborn screening checks thyroid-stimulating hormone (or thyroxine); untreated it causes intellectual disability and poor growth.

nodes.q: Why should you avoid removing or biopsying the tongue-base mass?
nodes.a: It may be the patient's only functioning thyroid tissue
nodes.note: Surgery would make her fully hypothyroid.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.note: Replacing the hormone also lowers thyroid-stimulating hormone, which shrinks the mass. Surgery or radioactive iodine is kept for bleeding or airway and swallowing problems.

nodes.q: A midline mass could suggest a thyroglossal duct cyst. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Midline neck mass below the hyoid that moves up with swallowing and tongue protrusion**; normal thyroid in the neck
**Mass at the tongue base behind the foramen cecum with iodine uptake there and none in the neck**

nodes.note: The trap: both come from the same duct.

nodes.q: Other swellings and causes of hypothyroidism were also possible. Which finding in her case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from her case
rows: **Lateral neck cyst along the front edge of the sternocleidomastoid**
**Bluish mucous cyst in the floor of the mouth beside the frenulum, no iodine uptake**
A swelling in the floor of the mouth that fails to take up iodine
**Doughy midline floor-of-mouth or neck cyst, no iodine uptake**
A doughy cyst without iodine uptake
**Firm goiter in the neck with anti-peroxidase antibodies**

nodes.note: Only lingual thyroid shows iodine uptake in the tongue and none in the neck.

root.stem: A 35-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has had 6 months of aching bones and itching. He is obese and has a diet of chocolate milk, cola, processed deli meat sandwiches and pizza. His blood pressure is 155/100 mm Hg. Serum creatinine is 4.1 mg/dL and serum phosphorus is 6 mg/dL.
root.oneliner: 35M + chronic kidney disease + 6 months of aching bones and itching + obese + diet of cola, deli meat, chocolate milk and pizza + BP 155/100 + creatinine 4.1 + phosphorus 6

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Secondary hyperparathyroidism due to chronic kidney disease
nodes.note: The parathyroid glands overwork to correct a low calcium. The clincher: **advanced chronic kidney disease with high phosphorus, low calcium, low 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D and high parathyroid hormone**.

nodes.q: Which pattern of parathyroid hormone synthesis, serum calcium and serum 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D is expected?
nodes.a: Parathyroid hormone synthesis up, calcium down, 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D down
nodes.note: Low calcium is the stimulus. The parathyroid glands become hyperplastic.

nodes.q: Why is 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D low?
nodes.a: The failing kidney cannot perform the 1-alpha-hydroxylation of 25-hydroxyvitamin D
nodes.note: Less vitamin D means less calcium absorbed from the gut.

nodes.q: Why is his phosphorus high?
nodes.a: The kidney excretes less phosphate as filtration falls
nodes.note: Phosphate binds calcium and lowers ionized calcium, and it also suppresses 1-alpha-hydroxylase; fibroblast growth factor 23 rises early. His cola, deli meat and processed foods add a heavy phosphate load.

nodes.q: What do his parathyroid glands look like?
nodes.a: All four glands are enlarged (diffuse hyperplasia)
nodes.note: A single enlarged gland (adenoma) is the usual cause of primary hyperparathyroidism.

nodes.q: Which bone disease results?
nodes.a: Renal osteodystrophy (osteitis fibrosa cystica, with osteoclast overactivity, brown tumors and a salt-and-pepper skull)
nodes.note: Bone aches and fractures follow.

nodes.q: Parathyroid hormone speeds bone resorption by binding its receptor on which cells?
nodes.a: Osteoblasts, which then release receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL) to activate osteoclasts
nodes.note: Osteoclasts have no parathyroid hormone receptor. Continuous high parathyroid hormone breaks bone down; intermittent dosing (teriparatide) builds it.

nodes.q: Which vascular and skin complication results from a high calcium-phosphate product?
nodes.a: Calciphylaxis (vascular calcification with painful skin necrosis)
nodes.note: It is also linked to cardiovascular death in kidney failure.

nodes.q: What is the first step in management?
nodes.a: Restrict dietary phosphate and give phosphate binders with meals
nodes.note: Binders such as sevelamer or calcium acetate. Vitamin D analogs (calcitriol) are added.

nodes.q: Which drug class lowers parathyroid hormone by sensitizing the calcium-sensing receptor?
nodes.note: Parathyroidectomy is for refractory disease.

nodes.q: High parathyroid hormone could suggest primary hyperparathyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High calcium, low phosphorus, normal kidney function**; usually a single adenoma; stones, bones, groans and psychiatric overtones
**Low or normal calcium with high phosphorus in advanced kidney disease**

nodes.note: The trap: both raise parathyroid hormone and cause bone disease.

nodes.q: Other causes of high parathyroid hormone were also possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Autonomous glands after years of kidney failure, with high calcium**
Years of dialysis or a kidney transplant
**Low 25-hydroxyvitamin D, low phosphorus, from poor intake or sun exposure**
Low phosphorus; here phosphorus is high

root.stem: An 80-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 25 years has had 2 months of severe constipation that over-the-counter laxatives have not relieved. He also feels light-headed on standing, vomits undigested food hours after meals and has erectile dysfunction. His pulse is 76/min both lying and standing. His abdomen is distended. His thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal, and colonoscopy shows no abnormalities.
root.oneliner: 80M + type 2 diabetes for 25 years + 2 months of severe constipation unrelieved by laxatives + light-headed on standing, fixed pulse 76 + vomiting undigested food hours after meals + erectile dysfunction + distended abdomen + normal TSH + normal colonoscopy
highlight: pulse is 76/min both lying and standing
vomits undigested food hours after meals
normal, and colonoscopy shows no abnormalities

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Long-standing diabetes damages the nerves that run the gut, heart, bladder and genitals. The clincher: **constipation with a normal colonoscopy plus other autonomic failure (orthostatic light-headedness with a fixed pulse, delayed gastric emptying, erectile dysfunction) in long-standing diabetes**.

nodes.q: Dysfunction of which nerves causes his constipation?
nodes.note: They carry parasympathetic fibers from S2 to S4 to the descending colon, sigmoid and rectum. The hypogastric nerve is sympathetic; the inferior rectal and perineal nerves are somatic branches of the pudendal nerve.

nodes.q: What injures the nerves?
nodes.a: Chronic hyperglycemia: sorbitol buildup, advanced glycation end products and ischemia of the small vessels that feed nerves
nodes.note: Aldose reductase turns glucose into sorbitol inside nerve cells.

nodes.q: Which stomach problem makes him vomit undigested food hours after meals?
nodes.a: Gastroparesis (delayed gastric emptying from vagal damage)
nodes.note: Gastric emptying scintigraphy confirms it.

nodes.q: Which drug speeds gastric emptying by blocking dopamine receptors?
nodes.note: Erythromycin, a motilin agonist, is an alternative. Metoclopramide can cause tardive dyskinesia.

nodes.q: What explains his light-headedness on standing with a pulse that does not rise?
nodes.a: Orthostatic hypotension from failure of the baroreceptor reflex (damaged sympathetic and vagal pathways)
nodes.note: Normally standing lowers pressure, the baroreceptors fire less, and sympathetic outflow raises the heart rate and constricts vessels. Here neither happens.

nodes.q: Which heart event can occur without chest pain in these patients?
nodes.note: Cardiac autonomic nerves are damaged, so pain is not felt.

nodes.q: Which bladder problem is expected from the same nerve damage?
nodes.a: An atonic bladder with urinary retention and overflow incontinence
nodes.note: Loss of parasympathetic input; erectile dysfunction comes from the same neuropathy.

nodes.q: Which warning symptom of low blood sugar may he lose if he takes insulin?
nodes.a: Adrenergic symptoms such as sweating and tremor (hypoglycemia unawareness)
nodes.note: Autonomic failure blunts the warning response.

nodes.q: Which measure slows progression of the neuropathy?
nodes.note: The benefit is clearest in type 1 diabetes; exclude other causes first.

nodes.q: Constipation in an older man could suggest hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cold intolerance, weight gain, bradycardia, dry skin and a high thyroid-stimulating hormone**
**Constipation with other autonomic failure (orthostatic light-headedness with a fixed pulse, erectile dysfunction) and a normal thyroid-stimulating hormone**

nodes.note: The trap: both cause constipation and fatigue in the old.

nodes.q: Other causes of constipation were also possible. Which finding in his case rules out each?

head: Look-alike
Clincher
Missing from his case
rows: **Weight loss, anemia, bleeding and a mass on colonoscopy**
**Failure to pass meconium in a newborn, no ganglion cells in the rectum**

nodes.note: Only diabetic autonomic neuropathy gives constipation with normal colonoscopy and other autonomic failure.

root.stem: A 29-year-old woman at 22 weeks' gestation has had 3 months of nervousness, heat intolerance, sweating and palpitations, with three loose stools a day and a weight gain of only 2 kg. Her pulse is 112/min and her blood pressure is 134/62 mm Hg. Her eyes look wide open and slightly bulging, her skin is warm and moist, and her outstretched fingers show a fine tremor. The thyroid gland is smooth, diffusely enlarged and not tender, with a soft whooshing sound heard over it, and the skin over both shins is thick and waxy. She has no nausea or vomiting, no neck pain, no headaches, and takes no medicines or supplements.
root.oneliner: 29F + 22 weeks pregnant + 3 months of nervousness, heat intolerance, sweating, palpitations + loose stools, poor weight gain + pulse 112 + wide bulging eyes + warm moist skin + fine tremor + smooth diffuse non-tender goiter with whooshing sound + thick waxy shins + no nausea or vomiting, no neck pain, no headaches, no medicines
highlight: smooth, diffusely enlarged and not tender

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: An autoimmune cause of an overactive thyroid. The clincher: **hyperthyroid symptoms + a smooth diffuse goiter with a bruit + bulging eyes and thick waxy shins**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Diffuse toxic goiter (Basedow disease in parts of Europe)
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which autoantibody drives the overactive gland?
nodes.a: Antibody that binds and stimulates the thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH, thyrotropin) receptor
nodes.note: A stimulating (type II hypersensitivity) antibody acts like TSH, so the whole gland grows and makes thyroid hormone without control. It is not an antibody against thyroglobulin or thyroid peroxidase (these point to Hashimoto thyroiditis), and the thyroid is not destroyed by cytotoxic T cells.

nodes.q: Which second messenger rises inside the thyroid cell when the receptor is stimulated?
nodes.a: Cyclic AMP (the TSH receptor is a Gs protein-coupled receptor)
nodes.note: Cyclic AMP drives iodide uptake, thyroid hormone synthesis, hormone release and growth of the gland.

nodes.q: What does the thyroid look like under the microscope?
nodes.a: Tall, crowded follicular cells with scalloped, pale colloid
nodes.note: Diffuse hyperplasia and hypertrophy of the follicles from constant receptor stimulation, with patchy lymphocytes. The thyroid peroxidase antibodies of Hashimoto thyroiditis can also be present, but the stimulating antibody is the cause.

nodes.q: The high thyroid hormone level lowers which hypothalamic hormone through negative feedback?
nodes.note: Pituitary TSH falls too. Thyroid iodide uptake and the peripheral conversion of thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine (T3) are increased, not decreased, and the TSH receptors on the gland are still present.

nodes.q: Through which type of receptor do thyroid hormones act inside cells?
nodes.a: Nuclear receptors that pair with the retinoid X receptor and bind DNA
nodes.note: They work like steroid hormones and change gene transcription, which is why effects (heart rate, heat production) are slow to start and slow to fade.

nodes.q: The same antibodies explain her bulging eyes and thick shins. Which material builds up in the orbit and the skin?
nodes.a: Glycosaminoglycans (hyaluronic acid) made by stimulated fibroblasts
nodes.note: Orbital fibroblasts and shin skin fibroblasts carry TSH receptors. The shin change is called pretibial myxedema; eye disease and skin disease can persist after the thyroid is treated.

nodes.q: Which blood test confirms an overactive thyroid?
nodes.a: Low TSH with a high free T4
nodes.note: In a woman with tremor, fast pulse, loose stools and poor weight gain in pregnancy, the first test is TSH. Measuring TSH receptor antibodies confirms Graves disease; a radioactive iodine uptake scan is avoided in pregnancy.

nodes.q: Which fast irregular heart rhythm is the common cardiac complication?
nodes.note: Thyroid hormone increases the number of beta-adrenergic receptors in the heart; chronic overload can also lead to high-output heart failure.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening flare of her disease can an infection, surgery or childbirth trigger?
nodes.note: Fever, delirium, severe tachycardia, atrial fibrillation and heart failure. Treatment (beta-blocker, propylthiouracil, then iodide, and a glucocorticoid) is a Step 2 detail.

nodes.q: How does methimazole lower thyroid hormone production?
nodes.a: It inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking iodide oxidation, organification and coupling
nodes.note: Propylthiouracil does this too and also blocks peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion.

nodes.q: Which blood complication must patients taking these drugs be warned about?
nodes.a: Agranulocytosis (fever or sore throat means stop the drug and check the white count)
nodes.note: Propylthiouracil can also cause liver failure.

nodes.q: Which antithyroid drug is preferred in the first trimester of pregnancy?
nodes.note: Methimazole can cause birth defects early in pregnancy; switch to methimazole after the first trimester. Beta-blockers control tremor and palpitations.

nodes.q: Which definitive treatment is contraindicated in pregnancy?
nodes.note: Outside pregnancy, definitive options are radioactive iodine or thyroidectomy; the fetal thyroid takes up iodine after about 10 weeks.

nodes.q: Which problem can her antibodies cause in the baby?
nodes.note: The immunoglobulin G antibodies cross the placenta and stimulate the fetal thyroid; check antibody titers in the third trimester.

nodes.q: Her symptoms in pregnancy could suggest gestational transient thyrotoxicosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **First trimester, with nausea and vomiting**, a rise in human chorionic gonadotropin that stimulates the TSH receptor; no goiter, eye signs or antibodies; settles by about 18 weeks
**22 weeks, symptoms persist, diffuse goiter with bruit, eye signs and TSH receptor antibodies**

nodes.note: The trap: both give a low TSH in pregnancy.

nodes.q: Early Hashimoto thyroiditis can cause a short overactive phase. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Firm, rubbery goiter + thyroid peroxidase and thyroglobulin antibodies**, no bruit or eye disease; becomes underactive later; lymphoid follicles and Hurthle cells
**Bruit, bulging eyes and thick shins + TSH receptor antibodies**; stays overactive until treated

nodes.q: Her goiter could suggest a toxic multinodular goiter. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Lumpy, nodular gland, usually older patient**; patchy radioactive iodine uptake; no eye signs or shin changes
**Smooth diffuse gland + eye signs + thick shins**; uniform radioactive iodine uptake

nodes.q: Her high thyroid hormone level could come from secret thyroxine tablets. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Small, non-enlarged gland + low radioactive iodine uptake + low thyroglobulin**; no eye signs
**Enlarged gland with a bruit + high radioactive iodine uptake** (outside pregnancy)

nodes.q: Her overactive thyroid could suggest a painful viral thyroiditis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Tender thyroid after a viral illness + high erythrocyte sedimentation rate + low radioactive iodine uptake**; no eye signs
**Painless smooth goiter + bulging eyes**; high uptake

nodes.q: Her palpitations and tremor could suggest pheochromocytoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Episodic headache, pounding heart and sweating with severe high blood pressure**; pale skin; high urine metanephrines; no goiter
**Constant symptoms + warm moist skin + goiter + low TSH**; wide pulse pressure rather than severe hypertension

nodes.q: Her nervousness and palpitations could suggest an anxiety disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Normal TSH, no goiter, cool clammy hands**; weight stable
**Low TSH + goiter + warm moist skin + weight loss or poor gain despite good appetite**

root.stem: A 7-day-old girl born at term is brought in because she is vomiting, feeding poorly and has become limp over 2 days. She has an enlarged clitoris and partly fused labia, with no testes felt. Her blood pressure is low and her mucous membranes are dry. Serum sodium is low, serum potassium is high, glucose is low and 17-hydroxyprogesterone is markedly raised, while cortisol is low. Her karyotype is 46,XX and a pelvic ultrasound shows a uterus. Her mother took no medicines during pregnancy and has no signs of male-pattern hair or voice change.
root.oneliner: 7-day-old F + vomiting, poor feeding, limp + enlarged clitoris, fused labia, no testes + low blood pressure, dehydration + low sodium, high potassium, low glucose + high 17-hydroxyprogesterone, low cortisol + 46,XX + uterus on ultrasound + mother took no medicines, no virilization
highlight: enlarged clitoris and partly fused labia
sodium is low, serum potassium is high

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Inherited block in cortisol production, causing androgen excess. The clincher: **a virilized 46,XX newborn + salt wasting + markedly raised 17-hydroxyprogesterone**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same disease.

nodes.q: Which enzyme is deficient in about 95% of cases?
nodes.note: It normally turns 17-hydroxyprogesterone into 11-deoxycortisol and progesterone into 11-deoxycorticosterone. The block stops both cortisol and aldosterone, so **17-hydroxyprogesterone piles up**.

nodes.q: How is it inherited?
nodes.note: The gene (CYP21A2) lies on chromosome 6 near the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes.

nodes.q: Which products are made in excess because the pathway is shunted?
nodes.note: They virilize the external genitalia of a female fetus. The uterus and ovaries are normal.

nodes.q: Which pituitary hormone rises because cortisol is low?
nodes.note: Loss of negative feedback from cortisol. High ACTH drives the adrenal cortex to grow and keeps pushing steroid precursors toward androgens.

nodes.q: What change in the adrenal cortex does the high ACTH cause?
nodes.note: More cortical cells make both adrenal glands larger.

nodes.q: A milder defect of the same enzyme shows up later in life. How does it usually present in a young woman?
nodes.a: Hirsutism, acne and irregular periods without salt wasting (nonclassic congenital adrenal hyperplasia)
nodes.note: Normal genitals at birth. Easily mistaken for polycystic ovary syndrome; an ACTH stimulation test shows an exaggerated 17-hydroxyprogesterone rise.

nodes.q: Which hormone deficiency explains her dehydration, low sodium and high potassium?
nodes.note: This is the salt-wasting form. A boy with the same defect has normal-looking genitalia and is found only when he vomits and becomes dehydrated in the first weeks.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening event can an infection or poor feeding trigger?
nodes.a: Adrenal crisis (shock, low glucose and high potassium that can cause arrhythmia)
nodes.note: Shock, low glucose and high potassium that can stop the heart. Emergency treatment is intravenous (IV) isotonic saline, dextrose and hydrocortisone (Step 2).

nodes.q: Which serum hormone is measured on newborn screening to detect it?
nodes.note: Measured on a heel-prick blood spot; an ACTH stimulation test confirms milder forms. Karyotype and pelvic ultrasound show a 46,XX infant with a uterus.

nodes.q: What is the long-term treatment?
nodes.note: Cortisol replacement lowers ACTH and so lowers the androgen excess; fludrocortisone replaces aldosterone. Give extra glucocorticoid during illness; plan genital reconstruction.

nodes.q: If untreated in childhood, which growth outcome appears?
nodes.a: Rapid early growth followed by short adult height (early closure of the growth plates)
nodes.note: Androgen excess also causes pubic hair and pseudo-precocious puberty.

nodes.q: Her virilization could suggest 11β-hydroxylase deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hypertension and low potassium**: 11-deoxycorticosterone builds up and acts as a mineralocorticoid, so renin and aldosterone are low; 11-deoxycortisol is high; dexamethasone lowers ACTH and brings 11-deoxycorticosterone, aldosterone and androgens back to normal
**Low blood pressure + salt wasting with high potassium + high 17-hydroxyprogesterone**

nodes.note: The trap: both virilize a 46,XX infant through ACTH-driven androgen excess.

nodes.q: Her abnormal steroid levels could suggest 17α-hydroxylase deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Hypertension and low potassium with low sex hormones**: a 46,XX girl has no puberty and is not virilized; a 46,XY child has female-looking genitals
**Virilized 46,XX infant with salt wasting and low blood pressure**

nodes.q: Her salt wasting could suggest 3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Salt wasting too, but **mild virilization in girls and undervirilization in boys; high dehydroepiandrosterone and 17-hydroxypregnenolone**
**Marked virilization of a 46,XX infant + high 17-hydroxyprogesterone**

nodes.q: Her ambiguous genitalia could suggest androgen insensitivity. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **46,XY with testes, no uterus**, high testosterone and normal electrolytes
**46,XX with a uterus and ovaries + high 17-hydroxyprogesterone + salt wasting**

nodes.q: Her ambiguous genitalia could suggest 5α-reductase deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **46,XY child with internal male structures**, normal electrolytes; high testosterone-to-dihydrotestosterone ratio; virilizes at puberty
**46,XX with a uterus + salt wasting**

nodes.q: Her virilization could come from androgens in the mother. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Maternal drug use or androgen-secreting tumor**; the infant has normal electrolytes and normal 17-hydroxyprogesterone; no progression after birth
**Mother took no medicines + salt wasting + high 17-hydroxyprogesterone**

nodes.q: Her vomiting and dehydration could suggest pyloric stenosis. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Usually a boy at 3-6 weeks; **projectile non-bilious vomiting, an olive-shaped mass, low chloride and low potassium with alkalosis**
**Day 7 + low sodium and high potassium + low glucose + abnormal genitalia**

root.stem: A 37-year-old woman has gained 18 kg over 6 months. She has a round face, a fat pad over the upper back and a large abdomen with thin arms and legs. Wide purple stripes cover the abdomen and flanks, and large bruises appear on the forearms after minor knocks. She has trouble rising from a chair and climbing stairs, and she has irregular periods and mild facial hair. Back pain began after lifting a light box, and a spine x-ray shows a compression fracture of a vertebra. Both ankles are mildly swollen. Her blood pressure is 190/95 mm Hg, fasting glucose is 138 mg/dL and serum potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. She takes no steroid tablets, creams, injections or inhalers. Plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) is below 5 pg/mL (reference below 120), 24-hour urinary free cortisol is four times normal, and the cortisol level does not fall after high-dose dexamethasone.
root.oneliner: 37F + 18 kg gain in 6 months + round face, upper back fat pad, big abdomen, thin limbs + wide purple striae + easy bruising + difficulty rising from a chair + irregular periods, mild facial hair + vertebral compression fracture after light lifting + ankle swelling + blood pressure 190/95 + glucose 138 + potassium 3.0 + no steroid use + low ACTH, high urinary cortisol, no suppression on high-dose dexamethasone
highlight: irregular periods and mild facial hair
takes no steroid tablets, creams, injections or inhalers
urinary free cortisol is four times normal
does not fall after high-dose dexamethasone

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Long-standing excess of cortisol. The clincher: **central obesity with thin limbs, moon face, wide purple striae, easy bruising, hypertension and proximal muscle weakness**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both terms describe the same state of cortisol excess.

nodes.q: Which cause of this syndrome is the most common overall?
nodes.note: Among endogenous causes, a pituitary ACTH adenoma (Cushing disease) is the most common; she takes no steroids and her ACTH is suppressed, so neither fits her.

nodes.q: Why are her arms and legs thin and her skin easily bruised while her trunk gains fat?
nodes.a: Cortisol breaks down protein in skin and muscle (catabolism) and redistributes fat to the trunk
nodes.note: Thin skin shows underlying vessels as purple striae and bruises easily; wasted thigh muscle explains why she cannot rise from a chair.

nodes.q: Which metabolic complication explains her raised glucose?
nodes.a: Insulin resistance with increased gluconeogenesis, leading to diabetes mellitus
nodes.note: Cortisol raises hepatic glucose output and blocks insulin action.

nodes.q: How does very high cortisol cause her high blood pressure, low potassium and ankle swelling?
nodes.a: It overwhelms 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 and activates the mineralocorticoid receptor
nodes.note: Normally 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2 inactivates cortisol in the kidney. The same effect explains edema in a child on long-term oral hydrocortisone: the drug binds both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid receptors, causing sodium retention, edema and hypokalemia.

nodes.q: Which osteoclast-activating signal does excess cortisol increase, explaining her vertebral fracture?
nodes.a: Increased expression of receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa-B ligand (RANKL), which prolongs osteoclast survival and activates them
nodes.note: Glucocorticoids also reduce osteoblast function and calcium absorption, so trabecular bone (spine, ribs) is lost first.

nodes.q: Because her ACTH is almost undetectable, which source of cortisol is the cause?
nodes.a: A cortisol-secreting tumor of the adrenal zona fasciculata
nodes.note: An adenoma or carcinoma. The zona glomerulosa makes aldosterone and the zona reticularis makes androgens. The other adrenal gland shrinks because the high cortisol switches off ACTH.

nodes.q: Which tests screen for cortisol excess?
nodes.a: 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol, or an overnight low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
nodes.note: Two abnormal tests confirm it. Then measure plasma ACTH: low ACTH means an adrenal source and calls for adrenal computed tomography (CT).

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Surgical removal of the adrenal tumor (adrenalectomy)
nodes.note: Benefits: lowers blood pressure, glucose and fracture risk.

nodes.q: Why does she need hydrocortisone cover after surgery?
nodes.a: The remaining adrenal gland is shrunken after long ACTH suppression
nodes.note: Risk of adrenal crisis until it recovers, which can take months.

nodes.q: Which complication is the main cause of death if untreated?
nodes.note: Hypertension, diabetes and clots all contribute; serious infections are the other major cause.

nodes.q: Her cortisol excess could be Cushing disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High or normal ACTH + cortisol suppressed by high-dose dexamethasone** + bilateral adrenal hyperplasia; pituitary magnetic resonance imaging shows an adenoma

split.a: Cushing syndrome from an adrenal tumor
split.note: **ACTH below 5 + no suppression on high-dose dexamethasone + adrenal mass**

nodes.note: The trap: both give the same body changes; ACTH separates them.

nodes.q: Her cortisol excess could suggest ectopic ACTH production. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Very high ACTH and cortisol, rapid onset, severe hypokalemia and skin darkening**; small cell lung carcinoma or carcinoid; no suppression on high-dose dexamethasone

split.a: Cushing syndrome from an adrenal tumor
split.note: **ACTH below 5 and gradual onset over months**

nodes.q: Her body changes could come from prolonged steroid medicines. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Prolonged steroid use** (for example asthma); low ACTH, and the adrenals are suppressed and small; synthetic steroids such as prednisone or dexamethasone are not measured as cortisol

split.a: Cushing syndrome from an adrenal tumor
split.note: **No steroid use + high urinary cortisol + adrenal mass**

nodes.q: Her weight gain could suggest simple obesity. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Fat distributed generally; **pink, thin striae at most, no bruising, no proximal weakness; normal cortisol tests**
**Wide purple striae + bruising + proximal weakness + abnormal cortisol tests**

nodes.q: Her irregular periods and facial hair could suggest polycystic ovary syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: Irregular periods and acne or hirsutism with **high androgens and polycystic ovaries**; normal cortisol tests; no muscle weakness or fractures
**Wide purple striae + bruising + proximal weakness + fracture + high urinary cortisol**

nodes.q: Her weight gain could suggest hypothyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, slow pulse and high thyroid-stimulating hormone**; no purple striae
**Wide purple striae + high blood pressure + bruising + high urinary cortisol**
