title: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

root.stem: A 62-year-old man has had 3 weeks of lethargy, headache, nausea and increasing confusion. He has smoked 40 pack-years and has a cough and a 6-kg weight loss. He takes no medicines, has no edema and no drop in blood pressure on standing, and his mucous membranes are moist. Serum sodium is 122 mEq/L, plasma osmolality is 262 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality is 480 mOsm/kg and urine sodium is 45 mEq/L. Creatinine, thyroid function tests and morning cortisol are normal.
root.oneliner: 62M + 3 weeks of lethargy, headache, nausea, confusion + 40 pack-years, cough, 6-kg weight loss + no medicines + no edema, no postural hypotension, moist mucous membranes + sodium 122, plasma osmolality 262, urine osmolality 480, urine sodium 45 + normal creatinine, thyroid tests and cortisol
highlight: lethargy, headache, nausea and increasing confusion
no edema and no drop in blood pressure on standing
thyroid function tests and morning cortisol are normal

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.a: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH)
nodes.note: Too much antidiuretic hormone (ADH, vasopressin) for the body's water balance. The clincher: **low plasma osmolality with inappropriately concentrated urine in a euvolemic patient with normal thyroid and adrenal function**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: Both names describe the same condition.

nodes.q: Which urine finding is inappropriate when plasma osmolality is low?
nodes.a: Urine osmolality higher than plasma osmolality
nodes.note: With low plasma osmolality, healthy kidneys make maximally dilute urine (below 100 mOsm/kg). His urine is concentrated and his urine sodium is above 40 mEq/L. Low urea and low uric acid are other clues.

nodes.q: Which hormone deficiencies must be excluded before making the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Both can also cause euvolemic hyponatremia; his thyroid tests and cortisol are normal.

nodes.q: What does the excess ADH do in the kidney?
nodes.a: It inserts aquaporin-2 water channels in the collecting duct through V2 receptors, so free water is reabsorbed
nodes.note: Retained water dilutes plasma sodium.

nodes.q: Why is he euvolemic rather than edematous?
nodes.a: The expanded volume raises sodium excretion in the urine, so sodium is lost along with the retained water
nodes.note: Atrial natriuretic peptide rises and aldosterone falls; so the urine sodium is high.

nodes.q: Which tumor most likely makes the ADH?
nodes.a: Small cell carcinoma of the lung
nodes.note: A paraneoplastic syndrome from a neuroendocrine lung tumor in a heavy smoker. Other causes: central nervous system disease (head injury, meningitis), lung infection and drugs such as selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, carbamazepine, vincristine and cyclophosphamide.

nodes.q: Which test is most likely to show the source?
nodes.a: Chest x-ray, then computed tomography (CT), showing a central lung mass
nodes.note: Small cell tumors typically arise centrally near the hilum.

nodes.q: Why is he confused?
nodes.a: Water moves into brain cells, causing cerebral edema
nodes.note: Severe or fast-falling hyponatremia leads to seizures, coma and herniation.

nodes.q: What is the initial treatment of chronic mild disease?
nodes.a: Fluid restriction and treatment of the cause
nodes.note: Severe symptoms (seizure, coma) need hypertonic 3% saline. Chronic cases may use salt tablets with a loop diuretic.

nodes.q: Which complication follows if sodium is corrected too fast?
nodes.note: Presents days later with quadriparesis, dysarthria and a locked-in state. Limit the rise to about 8 mEq/L per 24 hours (Step 2 detail).

nodes.q: Which drug class blocks the receptor that mediates the water retention?
nodes.note: Demeclocycline is another option; it causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

nodes.q: His low sodium could come from drinking too much water (psychogenic polydipsia). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dilute urine (osmolality below 100 mOsm/kg, specific gravity 1.002)** and low urine sodium

split.a: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
split.note: **Urine osmolality higher than plasma osmolality + urine sodium above 40**

nodes.note: The trap: both give low plasma sodium and osmolality in a euvolemic person.

nodes.q: His low sodium could suggest fluid loss from vomiting or diarrhea. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Dry mucous membranes, postural hypotension, raised urea and creatinine, urine sodium below 10 mEq/L**; a colonic villous adenoma is a classic cause

split.a: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
split.note: **Moist mucous membranes, no postural drop, normal creatinine, urine sodium above 40**

nodes.q: His abnormal urine concentration could suggest diabetes insipidus. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Huge volumes of dilute urine + thirst + high or high-normal serum sodium**

split.a: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
split.note: **Low serum sodium + concentrated urine**

nodes.q: His low sodium could suggest adrenal insufficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low cortisol, postural hypotension, high potassium, skin darkening in the primary form**

split.a: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
split.note: **Normal morning cortisol, no postural drop, normal potassium**

nodes.q: His low sodium could suggest heart or liver failure. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Edema, ascites, raised jugular venous pressure; urine sodium below 10**

split.a: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
split.note: **No edema + euvolemic + urine sodium above 40**

root.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had 6 months of attacks of pounding headache, palpitations and drenching sweats that last about 20 minutes and begin when she bends over or lifts. Between attacks her blood pressure is 124/80 mm Hg; during one it reached 185/115 mm Hg with a pale face. Her blood pressure has stayed high despite hydrochlorothiazide. A day after propranolol was started for the palpitations, she had a severe headache with blood pressure 214/132 mm Hg. Her father had medullary thyroid carcinoma. Her thyroid is normal on examination, there is no tremor, serum potassium is 4.2 mEq/L, blood pressure is equal in both arms and legs, and no abdominal bruit is heard. Plasma free metanephrines are four times the upper limit and a computed tomography (CT) scan shows a 2-cm right adrenal nodule.
root.oneliner: 32F + attacks of pounding headache, palpitations, drenching sweats for 20 minutes, triggered by bending or lifting + blood pressure 124/80 between, 185/115 during + hypertension despite hydrochlorothiazide + crisis a day after propranolol (214/132) + father with medullary thyroid carcinoma + normal thyroid, no tremor, potassium 4.2, equal arm and leg blood pressure, no abdominal bruit + metanephrines 4x normal + 2-cm adrenal nodule
highlight: pounding headache, palpitations and drenching sweats
begin when she bends over or lifts
equal in both arms and legs
free metanephrines are four times the upper limit

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A catecholamine-secreting tumor. The clincher: **attacks of headache, palpitations and sweating with paroxysmal hypertension, high metanephrines and an adrenal mass**.

nodes.q: Which cells does the tumor arise from?
nodes.a: Chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla
nodes.note: Derived from the neural crest. Outside the adrenal gland the same tumor is called a paraganglioma.

nodes.q: Which hormones does it release?
nodes.note: They are broken down to metanephrines and vanillylmandelic acid in the urine.

nodes.q: Which enzyme, induced by cortisol arriving from the adrenal cortex, turns norepinephrine into epinephrine?
nodes.note: This is why adrenal tumors can make epinephrine, while extra-adrenal paragangliomas make mainly norepinephrine. Tyrosine hydroxylase is the rate-limiting step of catecholamine synthesis.

nodes.q: What does the tumor look like under the microscope?
nodes.a: Nests of cells (Zellballen) that stain for chromogranin
nodes.note: Cells turn brown with chromium salts (the chromaffin reaction). The old "rule of 10s" underestimates inherited cases: about a third of patients carry a germline mutation, which is why every patient is offered genetic testing.

nodes.q: Which blood or urine test is the best screen?
nodes.a: Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines
nodes.note: Do this before imaging; then CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the adrenals. A metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan finds extra-adrenal tumors.

nodes.q: Which inherited syndrome fits her father's thyroid cancer?
nodes.note: Other associations: von Hippel-Lindau disease and neurofibromatosis type 1.

nodes.q: Why did a non-selective beta-blocker trigger a crisis?
nodes.a: Unopposed α-adrenergic vasoconstriction (β2 vasodilation was blocked)
nodes.note: Never give a beta-blocker before an alpha-blocker.

nodes.q: Which drug class must be started first?
nodes.note: Phenoxybenzamine blocks alpha receptors irreversibly. Add a beta-blocker only after adequate alpha blockade, to control tachycardia.

nodes.q: What is the definitive treatment?
nodes.a: Surgical removal of the tumor (laparoscopic adrenalectomy)
nodes.note: Done after 1-2 weeks of alpha blockade and volume loading.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening event can a catecholamine surge cause during induction of anesthesia or tumor handling?
nodes.a: Hypertensive crisis (stroke, arrhythmia or myocardial infarction)
nodes.note: Treatment is intravenous phentolamine or nitroprusside (Step 2 detail).

nodes.q: Her palpitations could suggest hyperthyroidism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Constant heat intolerance, tremor, goiter, weight loss and low thyroid-stimulating hormone**; wide pulse pressure
**Episodes of severe hypertension with headache and sweating**; normal thyroid; high metanephrines

nodes.note: The trap: both cause palpitations and sweating.

nodes.q: Her hypertension could suggest primary aldosteronism. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Constant hypertension + low potassium + metabolic alkalosis + undetectable renin**; no attacks
**Paroxysmal hypertension with headache and sweats + normal potassium**

nodes.q: Her hypertension could suggest renovascular disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Abdominal bruit + high renin + creatinine rise on an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor**; fibromuscular dysplasia in young women
**Paroxysmal symptoms + no bruit + high metanephrines**

nodes.q: Her high blood pressure in a young woman could suggest coarctation of the aorta. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Higher blood pressure in the arms than the legs, weak femoral pulses, rib notching**
**Equal arm and leg pressures + attacks + adrenal nodule**

nodes.q: Her attacks could suggest panic disorder. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Fear, shortness of breath and tingling during the attack**; normal metanephrines and normal adrenal imaging
**Pounding headache and sweating + trigger by bending + high metanephrines + adrenal mass**

root.stem: A 46-year-old man is brought in after fainting in the street. He has had 3 weeks of profuse watery diarrhea, up to 5 liters a day, which continues during a 48-hour fast, and his face is flushed. There is no blood in the stool, no recent travel, no abdominal pain and no history of ulcers. His blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg and his pulse is 118/min. A gastric aspirate contains almost no acid. Serum potassium is 2.1 mEq/L, bicarbonate is low, glucose is 150 mg/dL and calcium is mildly raised. Stool tests for ova, parasites and Clostridioides difficile are negative, the stool osmotic gap is low, and urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid is normal. A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a 4-cm mass in the tail of the pancreas.
root.oneliner: 46M + syncope + 3 weeks of watery diarrhea up to 5 L/day, persisting with fasting + flushed face + no blood, no travel, no abdominal pain, no ulcers + blood pressure 88/54, pulse 118 + almost no gastric acid + potassium 2.1, low bicarbonate, glucose 150, high calcium + negative ova, parasites, C. difficile + low stool osmotic gap + normal urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid + 4-cm pancreatic tail mass
highlight: watery diarrhea, up to 5 liters a day
no abdominal pain and no history of ulcers
4-cm mass in the tail of the pancreas

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor that makes vasoactive intestinal polypeptide. The clincher: **huge-volume watery diarrhea that continues during fasting + hypokalemia + low stomach acid (watery diarrhea, hypokalemia, achlorhydria: WDHA), with a pancreatic mass**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.a: Verner-Morrison syndrome (also called pancreatic cholera or WDHA syndrome)
nodes.note: Exam options may use any of the three names.

nodes.q: Which hormone does the tumor release?
nodes.note: It also relaxes smooth muscle (causing flushing), inhibits gastric acid, and raises glucose and calcium.

nodes.q: How does this hormone cause diarrhea?
nodes.a: It raises cyclic AMP in intestinal epithelial cells, driving chloride and water secretion
nodes.note: This secretory diarrhea has a stool osmotic gap below 50 mOsm/kg and does not stop with fasting.

nodes.q: From which pancreatic cell line does the tumor arise?
nodes.note: Most are in the body or tail; many are malignant and have already spread to the liver at diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which inherited tumor syndrome can include this tumor?
nodes.note: Pituitary, parathyroid and pancreatic islet tumors (the 3 Ps); the MEN1 gene encodes menin, a tumor suppressor. His raised calcium is usually from the tumor itself, but parathyroid disease should be looked for.

nodes.q: Which acid-base disturbance results from the stool losses?
nodes.note: Bicarbonate is lost in the stool.

nodes.q: What explains his fainting and low blood pressure?
nodes.note: Intravenous (IV) fluids come first.

nodes.q: Which lethal event can potassium 2.1 mEq/L cause?
nodes.note: U waves and flat T waves may appear first. Replace potassium with cardiac monitoring.

nodes.q: Which test confirms the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Then CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and a somatostatin-receptor scan to find the tumor and spread.

nodes.q: What is the first treatment?
nodes.a: IV fluids with potassium replacement, then octreotide
nodes.note: Surgical resection of the tumor is definitive when possible.

nodes.q: Which natural hormone does octreotide imitate?
nodes.note: It inhibits release of VIP and many other gut hormones, and stops the diarrhea.

nodes.q: His diarrhea from a pancreatic tumor could suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Excess gastric acid, severe peptic ulcers, pain**; diarrhea improves with a proton pump inhibitor; high gastrin
**Low or absent stomach acid + no ulcers + watery diarrhea during fasting + hypokalemia**

nodes.note: The trap: both are pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors causing diarrhea.

nodes.q: His flushing and diarrhea could suggest carcinoid syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Flushing + wheeze + right-sided heart valve disease + high urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid**; liver metastases
**Normal urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid + large-volume diarrhea + hypokalemia**

nodes.q: His rice-water-like diarrhea could suggest cholera. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Recent travel or contaminated water; acute rice-water stool**, positive stool culture; resolves within days
**No travel + 3 weeks + pancreatic mass**

nodes.q: His raised glucose with a pancreatic mass could suggest a glucagonoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Necrolytic migratory erythema + weight loss + very high glucagon**; no watery diarrhea
**Watery diarrhea + hypokalemia; no rash**

root.stem: A 48-year-old man has had 4 months of headaches, muscle weakness and cramps, and he wakes twice a night to urinate. His blood pressure is 172/98 mm Hg and he has no edema. Serum sodium is 144 mEq/L, potassium is 2.4 mEq/L, bicarbonate is 33 mEq/L and creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL. Arterial pH is 7.46. Morning cortisol is normal, and plasma renin activity is undetectable. He has no headaches with sweating or palpitations and no Cushingoid appearance.
root.oneliner: 48M + 4 months of headaches, muscle weakness, cramps, nocturia + blood pressure 172/98, no edema + sodium 144, potassium 2.4, bicarbonate 33, pH 7.46, creatinine 1.0 + normal morning cortisol + undetectable renin + no sweating, palpitations or Cushingoid look
highlight: wakes twice a night to urinate
no headaches with sweating or palpitations

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: Autonomous aldosterone production; the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension. The clincher: **hypertension + hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis with undetectable renin**.

nodes.q: The exam may list it under another name. What is it?
nodes.note: The name is used for primary hyperaldosteronism, historically for the aldosterone-producing adenoma.

nodes.q: How does aldosterone excess produce low potassium and alkalosis?
nodes.a: It increases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct and drives potassium and hydrogen ion secretion
nodes.note: Principal cells take up sodium through epithelial sodium channels (ENaC) and secrete potassium; intercalated cells secrete hydrogen.

nodes.q: Why is renin undetectable?
nodes.a: Sodium and water retention expands volume and switches off renin
nodes.note: Hence the high aldosterone-to-renin ratio.

nodes.q: Why does he have no edema despite sodium retention?
nodes.a: Aldosterone escape (pressure natriuresis and atrial natriuretic peptide)
nodes.note: Sodium is lost again after a few days, so volume expansion plateaus.

nodes.q: Which electrolyte disturbance explains his muscle weakness and cramps?
nodes.note: Low potassium hyperpolarizes muscle cells and makes them less excitable; severe hypokalemia can progress to paralysis and rhabdomyolysis.

nodes.q: Why does the low potassium make him pass urine at night?
nodes.a: It impairs the kidney's ability to concentrate urine (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus)
nodes.note: The collecting duct responds poorly to antidiuretic hormone (ADH) when potassium is low.

nodes.q: Which electrocardiogram wave appears with this potassium level?
nodes.note: Followed by ventricular arrhythmia if severe.

nodes.q: Which test screens for it?
nodes.note: Stop spironolactone first; confirm with saline suppression, then adrenal computed tomography (CT).

nodes.q: Which adrenal zone makes the excess aldosterone?
nodes.a: Zona glomerulosa (from an adenoma or bilateral hyperplasia)
nodes.note: Hyperplasia is a little more common than a single adenoma.

nodes.q: Which test tells a one-sided adenoma from bilateral hyperplasia?
nodes.note: One-sided aldosterone excess means surgery can cure.

nodes.q: What is the treatment for a one-sided adenoma?
nodes.note: Blood pressure and potassium improve.

nodes.q: Which drug blocks the aldosterone receptor?
nodes.note: Spironolactone (or eplerenone, which is more selective for the mineralocorticoid receptor) is the treatment for bilateral hyperplasia. Hyperkalemia is a risk, so monitor potassium.

nodes.q: Which side effect of spironolactone comes from its blockade of androgen receptors?
nodes.note: Eplerenone avoids this.

nodes.q: His high aldosterone could come from renal artery stenosis (secondary hyperaldosteronism). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High renin** with high aldosterone; renal artery stenosis, heart failure or cirrhosis; edema in the latter two
**Undetectable renin + no edema**

nodes.note: The trap: both give hypertension, low potassium and alkalosis.

nodes.q: His hypertension and low potassium could suggest Cushing syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **High cortisol, central obesity, wide purple striae and bruising**
**Normal cortisol + normal body + undetectable renin**

nodes.q: His headaches and hypertension could suggest a pheochromocytoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Episodic headache, palpitations and sweating + high metanephrines**; potassium usually normal
**Constant hypertension + low potassium + undetectable renin**

nodes.q: His electrolyte changes could suggest an adrenal problem in the opposite direction, Addison disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Low cortisol, low blood pressure, high potassium, low sodium**
**Normal cortisol + high blood pressure + low potassium**

nodes.q: His hypertension could suggest chronic kidney disease. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Raised creatinine and urea, anemia, high or normal renin**, potassium normal or high
**Normal creatinine + undetectable renin + low potassium**

root.stem: A 55-year-old man has had 2 months of poor appetite, a 9-kg weight loss and a red, blistering rash in the groin and under the arms that crusts, heals and then returns in new areas. His tongue is sore and red, and the corners of his mouth are cracked. Fasting glucose is 280 mg/dL, hemoglobin is 10.2 g/dL with normal red cell size, and plasma glucagon is 1,500 pg/mL (reference 20 to 100). A computed tomography (CT) scan shows a 4-cm mass in the pancreas. He has had no episodes of low blood sugar, no watery diarrhea, no gallstones and no ulcer pain.
root.oneliner: 55M + 2 months of poor appetite, 9-kg weight loss + migratory crusting rash in groin and axillae + sore red tongue, cracked mouth corners + glucose 280 + normocytic anemia + glucagon 1,500 + 4-cm pancreatic mass + no hypoglycemia, watery diarrhea, gallstones or ulcer pain
highlight: red, blistering rash in the groin and under the arms
crusts, heals and then returns in new areas
no episodes of low blood sugar

nodes.q: What is the diagnosis?
nodes.note: A glucagon-secreting pancreatic tumor. The clincher: **a migratory blistering rash in the groin and armpits + weight loss + diabetes + very high glucagon**.

nodes.q: What is the name of the rash?
nodes.note: Red patches that blister, crust and heal in a moving pattern, in the groin, buttocks and around the mouth. Low amino acid levels and zinc deficiency are thought to contribute.

nodes.q: From which islet cell type does the tumor arise?
nodes.note: Usually in the body or tail of the pancreas; most are malignant with liver spread by the time of diagnosis.

nodes.q: Which inherited tumor syndrome can include this tumor?
nodes.note: Pituitary, parathyroid and pancreatic islet tumors (the 3 Ps).

nodes.q: Which process is occurring in his liver because of the excess glucagon?
nodes.a: Partial oxidation of fatty acids (ketone body production)
nodes.note: Glucagon inhibits acetyl-CoA carboxylase, so malonyl-CoA falls and carnitine acyltransferase I lets fatty acids enter mitochondria. It also raises glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis, and glycogen synthesis falls.

nodes.q: Which liver process, building new glucose from amino acids, does the excess glucagon drive?
nodes.note: Together with glycogen breakdown this raises his glucose. Using up amino acids lowers their blood levels, which is thought to feed the rash.

nodes.q: Why has he lost so much weight?
nodes.a: Glucagon-driven breakdown of protein and fat (catabolism)
nodes.note: The same process lowers amino acids.

nodes.q: Which blood abnormality is typical?
nodes.note: Chronic disease and suppressed red cell production.

nodes.q: Which life-threatening vascular complication is a known risk?
nodes.a: Deep vein thrombosis with pulmonary embolism
nodes.note: Glucagonoma has one of the highest rates of venous clots among neuroendocrine tumors.

nodes.q: Which tests confirm it?
nodes.a: Markedly raised fasting plasma glucagon (above 500 pg/mL), then CT or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
nodes.note: A skin biopsy of the rash shows superficial necrolysis.

nodes.q: What is the treatment?
nodes.a: Surgical resection of the tumor, with octreotide for symptom control
nodes.note: Zinc and amino acid replacement help the rash. Anticoagulate for clots.

nodes.q: His pancreatic islet tumor could be an insulinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Episodes of hypoglycemia relieved by food (Whipple triad)** + high C-peptide; weight gain
**Hyperglycemia + weight loss + migratory rash**

nodes.note: The trap: both are pancreatic islet tumors that change the blood glucose.

nodes.q: His weight loss with a pancreatic tumor could suggest a VIPoma (vasoactive intestinal polypeptide tumor). How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Watery diarrhea during fasting + hypokalemia**; no rash
**Rash + diabetes + anemia; no watery diarrhea**

nodes.q: His diabetes with a pancreatic tumor could suggest a somatostatinoma. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Diabetes + gallstones + fatty stools (steatorrhea)**; no rash
**Migratory rash + very high glucagon; no gallstones**

nodes.q: His pancreatic tumor could suggest Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Severe peptic ulcers + diarrhea + high gastrin**
**Rash + diabetes + weight loss + no ulcer pain**

nodes.q: His rash could suggest zinc deficiency. How do you tell them apart?

split.note: **Rash around the mouth, genitals and hands + diarrhea + hair loss**; low serum zinc; normal glucagon
**Migratory erythema + pancreatic mass + glucagon 1,500**
